(…)       Traditional media outlets have tried to accommodate and control the influx of information from these communities of contributors, in which news publication is a process, not a product (Beckett, 2008). As both traditional news media shift to an online format and citizen journalism becomes increasingly active and vocal, Beckett sees the future of journalism in this intersection between traditional media outlets, technological advance, and citizen journalists (ibid).      However, some caveats are in order, because while the changes in the media are real, they are not necessarily as revolutionary sometimes depicted. The “legacy” or traditional media (described here as newspaper, television, radio, print publishing, music and movies) coexist with “myriad” names for social media in the news world (Cohn, 2007). Similarly, the job categories may be permeable, with the professional journalist who uses new media technology to product news and information products working in parallel with the “citizen journalist” who contributes to an overall journalistic discourse by commenting on blog posts and submitting cell phone photos relevant to media outlets (ibid).       Computer-aided information collection, filtration, and presentation may help improve journalism and publication, but does not necessarily represent a break with the past. What technology has done is speed up the rate of production and distribution immeasurably, and also brought diverse methods of presentation together. Hence, internally, a news story package of a Web site may use both the spoken and written word, as well as music, moving and still images, graphic animations, including interactive hypertextual elements; and externally, the same package may be distributed or linked through a Web site, a Usenet group, email, SMS, MMS, radio, television, and print newspapers and magazines (Deuze, 2004). This fast, multifaceted approach to publishing is highly dynamic, requiring reevaluation of the roles of traditional journalists and editors and the environment in which they publish, as well as providing increased employment opportunities for the technically savvy.       As the old order changes, some key questions remain the same, in particular about the control and verification of the validity of published information. The argument is not wholly academic. Wikis in general, and Wikipedia in particular, stands as the most popular examples of open-access peer publishing on the Internet, providing people alternatives to more professional forms of scholarship or current events. But even for this examplar of peer publication, control is still exerted, especially on the most controversial articles, in an attempt to maintain the integrity of the information and prevent page defacement, a practice that contradicts the ideals the organization espouses (Angwin and Fowler, 2009) but provides a strong argument for the value of the editorial role.      The open-source movement is commonly associated with the fields of software and information technology. Made popular by Red Hat, Novell, and other Linux kernel innovators, open-source software (OSS) development has become a multibillion-dollar industry, encouraging the spread of the open-business model to many other industries. OSS complies with criteria regarding freely accessible source code, redistribution, and nonrestrictive licensing and involves tight feedback loops between production and consumption, with interesting dynamics of social-capital formation and skill development through remixing and sharing. (Bollier, 2006)       The open-source movement epitomizes the collaborative community discussed elsewhere (…) and covers a much wider spectrum than OSS. The Open Source Initiative, a nonprofit corporation that educates about and advocates for the benefits of open source, frequently uses the language of community, collaboration, and networks when discussing its goals and values.       Supporters of the open-source movement argue that the creation of new knowledge requires the free exchange of ideas, and the intellectual-property laws and digital methods of controlling or locking information are a threat to cultural and social creativity (Berry et al., 2008). Innovation is improved due to access to a steadily richer innovation commons (Hippel, 2005). Some researchers propose an incentive related to career concerns, in which open-source programmers are motivated to produce open-source works because future employers may see their work, or an ego-gratification incentive in which programmers desire recognition for their individual contribution (Lerner and Tirole, 2002). However, others argue that such an individualistic or profit-driven incentive is not the typical or primary motivation for open-source collaboration (Goetz, 2003; Benkler, 2006).      Commons-based open-peer production, which relies on decentralized information gathering and exchange, is a new model of production that often results in more efficient allocation of human creativity than in traditional firms (Benkler, 2004). This can result in a balancing act, as online communities and businesses explore each other, “trying to find effective ways to balance profit imperatives with the social and psychic needs of the commons” (Bollier, 2006: 40).       Gadman and Cooper describe open-source processes in utopian terms, equivalent to complex ecosystems of interactive relationships among people, institutions, and supporting structures, which require the cultivation of positive effects in the lives of those involved. They describe the facility enabled by open source as having the following components: making it easier for people to have equal access to information, resources, and tools; enabling rich interconnections of shared interests and capabilities; and creating a sense of ownership over outcomes and a sense of identity as people who improve their own lives and those of others. The first component is essentially human capital, the second is social capital, and the third is empowered autonomy.      An integral ingredient to the success of open-source collaboration is that technology has allowed for the convergence of a greater diversity of perspectives because traditional barriers to collaboration such as time and geography have been overcome. Even the less-traditional barriers of conceptual distances ae also overcome when specialists are taken out of their homogeneous communities and put into a group with a diverse skill set collaborating on a common goal to produce the most valuable output. (Fischer, 2005)      Open innovation presents several opportunities for positive economic growth. First, when companies embrace the open innovation model, they can begin to unlock some of their unused patents, allowing other firms to capitalize on those developments and offering the potential for the creation of new developments. A second benefit is the creation of employment opportunities for individuals and small enterprises. From the innovator’s perspective (the creator of the patent), a large and growing market exists for small R&D organizations and individuals. These small companies work to generate innovations in hopes of being acquired, or having their patents licenses or purchased by a larger organization. This effect is common in the pharmaceutical or computer-technology industries, but also can be found in video gaming, information technology, consumer products, biotechnology and other life sciences. (…)       With the relative novelty of open-source software development, there are few statistics that accurately depict the size and trends of the overall marketplace. Companies that engage in OSS development and sales are, with few exceptions, small privately held companies that do not report revenues or volume of deliveries. There are exceptions, including Red Hat and Novell, both of which are public. But overall this leaves market analysts in the position of simply estimating the numbers of users of open-source products, and estimating the potential revenue generated by such users. This is not an exercise in precision. For example, the Open Source Initiative – the open source community recognized body that advocates and governs open-source development activity – has estimated the number of Linux users to be anywhere between 4 million and 27 million. (Open Source Initiative, 2007) For this reason, this section does not try to estimate the market size or revenues for open-source processes, in particular as the term is loosely defined. Instead it focuses on the business model for software development, the large OSS companies, and the prospect of job creation in the OSS marketplace. (…)      The unique dynamics of OSS development allow for different market strategies. Since the software is, by definition, open to modify, use, or sell, the cost at which a company or individual acquires an open-source program will typically be minimal, or even free (Open Source Initiative, 2007). This situation is largely due to the microeconomic laws of zero economic profit: in a perfectly competitive market, a product will sell only for as much as its lowest-priced identical competitor (Allen et al., 2009). The limited, or nonexistent, barriers to entry in the OSS market create this perfectly competitive landscape. Open-source vendors, therefore, typically generate revenue from the goods and services that accompany the software. These include service packages and subscription, and enterprise consulting (McGovern, 2009). National Council on Disability (NCD). October 04th 2011. The Power of Digital Inclusion: Technology’s Impact on Employment Opportunities for People with Disabilities. See Pages 20 – 131. Retrievable here.: https://www.ncd.gov/assets/uploads/reports/2011/ncd-digital-inclusion-2011.pdf     [xii] Emma Roberts knows that her new Prime Video movie, “Space Cadet,” is an easy target for critics and cynics. “It’s earnest,” she says on “Just for Variety” podcast. “And people are probably going to make fun of that, but it’s like, you know what, whatever. I think that it’s better to be earnest and do your best and be proud of what you do, not matter the reception. (…) That’s why when people are so quick to see a movie or a show and they’re like, ‘Oh, I hate that,’ I’m like, ‘That was months and years and blood, sweat, tears.’ Producing stuff has made me realize you can’t really hate anything because it means that people have really, really, really tried and succeeded. If you’re watching something then that’s a success. (…) I’m not intimated by failure, and I’m not intimated by people having negative thoughts about something. I personally really loved ‘Madame Web.’ I really enjoyed the movie. I thought everyone in it was great. The director, S.J. Clarkson, I think did an amazing job. She’s the reason I wanted to do that movie. If it wasn’t for internet culture and everything being made into a joke, I think that the reception would’ve been different. (…) We’ve just cultivated this hate culture towards celebrities and towards movies and television online. Where it used to be like five people reviewed a movie, now it’s like you have people that won’t even say what their real name is saying how much they hate something. I’m like, “At least everyone should have to put their driver’s licenses number into their Instagram account, so you’d probably think twice before you said something rude if we had your driver’s license info.” (…) This Q&A has been edited and condensed. Emma Roberts on “Space Cadet,” Blaming the Internet for ‘Madame Web’ Flopping and Being Protected as a Nickelodeon Child Star. Variety.: https://variety.com/2024/film/columns/emma-roberts-space-cadet-madame-web-nickelodeon-1236060064/     [xiii] Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker has aggravated one of the internet’s biggest culture wars by telling a class of college graduates that one of the “most important” titltes a woman can hold is homemaker. (…) Drawing the most viral backlash this week, however, was a section of his speech in which he addressed the female graduates specifically – telling them that it’s women who have had “the most diabolical lies” told to them. “How many of you are sitting here now, about to cross this stage, and are thinking about all the promotions and titles you are going to get in your career? Some of you may go on to lead successful careers in the world,” Butker said. “But I would venture to guess that the majority of you are most excited about your marriage and the children you will bring into this world.” The criticisms that followed took aim at Butker as well as the NFL. (…) Butker’s comments share similarities with some of the more extreme ideas around gender roles that have gained traction in communities that promote “tradwife” lifestyles or other relationship dynamics that center on traditional gender roles. (…) A spokesperson for the NFL told People Magazine that Butker “gave a speech in his personal capacity” and his “views are not those of the NFL as an organization. The NFL is steadfast in our commitment to inclusion, which only makes our league stronger,” a spokesperson told the publication. (…) Butker, who is teammates with Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce, further drew surprise and criticism when he quotes Kelce’s girlfriend, Taylor Swift, whose monumental career success as a global pop star has inspired college courses. Chief’s Harrison Butker blasted for commencement speech encouraging women to be homemakers. NBC News.: https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/harrison-butker-kansas-city-chiefs-backlash-benedictine-college-speech-rcna152433   Harrison Butker (…) went to address the female graduates in the room directly. “For the ladies present today, congratulation on an amazing accomplishment,” he began. “I want to speak directly to you briefly because I think it is you, the women, who have had the most diabolical lies told to you.” Butker continued, “Some of you may go on to lead successful careers in the world, but I would venture to guess that the majority of you are most excited about your marriage and the children you will bring into this world.” (…) Speaking about his wife, Butker said, “I can tell that my beautiful wife, Isabell, would be the first to say her life truly started when she started living her vocation as a wife and as a mother.” He said that he is “beyond blessed” because Isabelle “would convert to the faith, become my wife, and embrace one of the most important titles of all: Homemaker.” “Isabelle’s dream of having a career might not have come true, but if you ask her today if she has any regrets on her decision, she would laugh out loud without hesitation, and say, ‘Hey, no.’” Chiefs’ Harrison Butker Criticized for Graduation Speech Attacking Working Women While Quoting Taylor Swift. People.: https://people.com/chiefs-harrison-butker-criticized-graduation-speech-attacking-working-women-quoting-taylor-swift-8648547              [xiv] Universities have entered their “Taylor Swift Era.” While there’s no degree for being a Swiftie, universities across the country are embracing the 14-time Grammy award-winning singer and are offering courses inspired by the superstar and her music catalog. BestColleges combed through the course catalogs and found classes empowering students to explicate Swift’s lyrics, analyze her albums era by era, and examine the societal impact of her hits. Here’s our syllabus of colleges and classes helping students study Taylor Swift and her music, impact and success. (…)       Stanford University is no stranger to Swiftie-designed classes. During the 2023 winter quarter, the university offered “All Too Well (Ten Week Version),” a course that featured an in-depth analysis of Swift’s hit “All Too Well,” led by students in the Italic arts program. This spring, Stanford offered students the chance to study “The Last Great American Songwriter: Storytelling With Taylor Swift Through the Eras.” Stanford student Ava Jeffs taught the class. She told BestColleges that she was inspired by courses at other schools and wondered if she could build a Swift-centered class at her university. “I created a syllabus over a couple of months and then sent it out to a bunch of professors because I really didn’t know how the process worked,” she said. “Eventually, one of the professors in the English Department told me that he liked my syllabus and he’d be willing to sponsor a class as a sort of student-initiate course.” Each week, students explored a different album, studying Swift’s storytelling techniques through each era, Jeffs said. Students examined each of her albums to learn about what that era or album represents in terms of its themes, motifs, literary references within the songs, how different songs connect to a broader storyline, and where the album – or era – fits into her broader discography.       So far, these universities have announced they will offer courses based on the singer in 2024:       “Musical storytelling with Taylor Swift and other iconic female artists,” at the University of Florida       “Ms. Americana: Taylor Swift on Ethics and Society” at Brigham Young University.       “Fandom in the US: Taylor Swift” at Bowling Green State University.       “Artistry, Policy & Entrepreneurship: Taylor Version” at the University of California, Berkeley.       “Data Enchanted: Transforming Numbers into Knowledge” at the University of Delaware.       “The Mastermind of the Taylor Swift Brand” at the University of Miami      “Cultural Studies and Popular Art” at the University of South Florida      “English 1500 : Taylor’s Version” at East Carolina University       “Gender / Media (Taylor’s Verson)” at the University of Tennessee      “Swiftonomics : Economics of Taylor Swift” at American University       “Taylor Swift, Gender and Communication” at Pennsylvania State University, Berks.       “Philosophy: Taylor Verson,” “Topics in Writing Studies: Taylor Swift,” and “Topics in Popular Music: Taylor Swift,” at the University of Cincinnati       “Intertextuality – Taylor’s Version” at Duke University       Colorado State University announced its offering the day before the release of Swift’s 11th studio album, “The Tortured Poets Department..” The summer course, entitled “Spanish for Swifty Purposes (Taylor Version).” will be taught by Assistant Professor for Spanish Specific Purposes Alyssia Miller De Rutte. (…)      Arizona State University offered a Swift-inspired course taught by a student last fall. Alexandra Wormley, a graduate student at Arizona State, announced she would be teaching her Taylor Swift class the same day “Speak Now: Taylor Version” was released.       Students at the Berklee College of Music in Boston also had the opportunity to dive into Swift’s ability to write chart-topping hits during the fall 2023 semester. “Songs of Taylor Swift” focused on Swift’s song composition and lyrics, according to the Boston Globe.       In addition, Rice University in Houston and the University of Delaware offered course on the singer. Rice’s course focused on the lyrical evolution and personal growth. The course took students through each of Swift’s albums in chronological order, focusing on topics such as femininity and gender; social media and public opinion; politics and social impact; fiction and nonfiction; American nationalism and whiteness; and family and feuds, according to the course listing.       Earlier the University of Missouri last spring offered the class “Taylor Swift: History & Literature Through Taylor Swift” in Spring 2023. The University of Texas at Austin and New York University’s Clive Davis Institute also taught courses covering her music in 2022. You Can Study Taylor Swift at These Colleges. Best Colleges.: https://www.bestcolleges.com/news/these-colleges-have-taylor-swift-classes/#:~:text=%22Songs%20of%20Taylor%20Swift%22%20focused,offered%20courses%20on%20the%20singer.             [xv] The freshmen retention rate applied to first-time / full-time students who come back for their second year. With 70% students making it past their freshmen year, Sarah Lawrence has freshmen retention rates similar to the national average. Nationwide, the average first to second year retention rate is 70.57%. When looking at just colleges and universities in New York, the average is 73.51%. College Factual.: https://www.collegefactual.com/colleges/sarah-lawrence-college/academic-life/graduation-and-retention/       [xvi] In many cases, 1 in 3 first-year students or more won’t make it back for sophomore year. The reasons run the gamut from family problems and loneliness to academic struggles and a lack of money. If schools you’re considering have low freshman retention rates, you’ll want to ask the admissions office why. Some colleges do a great job of taking care of their freshmen; some don’t. Hello, 
   
 I am writing to submit a public records request regarding communications between San Francisco city workers in your department and representatives of some companies. 
 Specifically, I am requesting copies of all communications, electronic or otherwise, between San Francisco city officials/employees/workers and officials/employees/workers and the organisation Limitless Specialty Services LLC, also known as Limitless Specialty Services, or  LSS, as well as Limitless Speciality Services Associates LLC, a related company. This includes emails, records of phone calls, minutes from meetings, and any other documentation that appears relevant to this request. The request goes from February 1, 2018 to the present day, June 1, 2019. 
  I am also requesting copies of all communications, electronic or otherwise, between San Francisco city officials/employees/workers and officials/employees/workers and the organisation MPPR Associates LLC, also known as MPPR Associates, or MPRR. This includes emails, records of phone calls, minutes from meetings, and any other documentation that appears relevant to this request. The request goes from May 1, 2011 to the present day, June 1, 2019. 
  I am also requesting copies of all communications, electronic or otherwise, between San Francisco city officials/employees/workers and officials/employees/workers and the organisation/company Weststreet. Sometimes employees/workers of the other organisations above refer to this corporate name. but this This includes emails, records of phone calls, minutes from meetings, and any other documentation that appears relevant to this request. The request goes from May 1, 2011 to the present day, June 1, 2019. They may use the email address format [name]@weststreet.org or [name]@weststreet.com, but this is not guaranteed, and the search should not be limited to this only. 
 I ask for a determination on this request within 10 days of your receipt of it, and an even prompter reply if you can make that determination without having to review the record[s] in question. 
 If you determine that any or all or the information qualifies for an exemption from disclosure, I ask you to note whether, as is normally the case under the Act, the exemption is discretionary, and if so whether it is necessary in this case to exercise your discretion to withhold the information. 
 If you determine that some but not all of the information is exempt from disclosure and that you intend to withhold it, I ask that you redact it for the time being and make the rest available as requested. 
 In any event, please provide a signed notification citing the legal authorities on which you rely if you determine that any or all of the information is exempt and will not be disclosed. 
 If not all the records requested are held, I ask that you provide that which is. 
 If I can provide any clarification that will help expedite your attention to my request, please contact me at robaeprice@gmail.com.  
 I am a journalist, and this request is being made for non-commercial, news-gathering purposes. 
 I ask that you notify me of any duplication costs exceeding $20 before you duplicate the records so that I may decide which records I want copied. I prefer digital copies if possible. 
 Thank you for your time and attention! 
 Sincerely, 
   
 Rob Price 
 News Editor, Business Insider 
 535 Mission Street, 14th Floor, San Francisco, CA 94105 
 robaeprice@gmail.com 
 +1 (650) 636-6268

NextRequest # 23-2715 IMMEDIATE DISCLOSURE REQUEST FOR PUBLIC RECORDS:  Second or Third Records Request for the LHH QIE’s Third “RCA” Report and Associated New “Action Plan” Milestones       May 31, 2023      Grant Colfax   Director of Public Health   City and County of San Francisco   101 Grove Street   San Francisco, CA  94102      Roland Pickens    Acting Executive Administrator    Laguna Honda Hospital   375 Laguna Honda Boulevard    San Francisco, CA  94116       Dear Dr. Colfax and Mr. Pickens,      This is an Immediate Disclosure Request for Public Records under San Francisco’s Sunshine Ordinance, the California Public Records Act, Proposition 59, and the Brown Act.      On May 10 I placed records request 23-2509 specifically asking for two documents: The LHH QIE’s third Root Cause Analysis (RCA) report and the QIE’s fourth 90-Day Monitoring Survey report dated May 10.      Six days later the NextRequest staff provided only the fourth 90-Day Monitoring Survey report dated May 10 on May 16, and didn’t say anything about the status of the other document, the third Root Cause Analysis (RCA) report.     The thrid Form 2567 for the Health Survey component of the second 90-Day Monitoring Survey that concluded on March 17, 2023 — a CMS abbreviated monitoring survey with an extended survey — was released and provided to me on May 18     Presumably, the QIE must also have received the third Form 2567 from the inspection that concluded on March 17, 2023, and should have by now completed the third Root Cause Analysis (RCA) report along with any new “Action Plan” milestones as a result of the third Root Cause Analysis (RCA) report. I’ve also requested several times in e-mails to Michaela Varisto for the third Root Cause Analysis (RCA) reportbut she has failed to respond to at least follow-up e-mails to her.     After all it should not have taken the QIE two months — between March 17 and now May 31 — to write and submit the third RCA report to CMS, and I should not have had to ask now two or three times for that third RCA report!      I have also submitted this new records request through NextRequest; it’s number is #23-2715.      For this new records request, please provide:          1.     The third Root Cause Analysis (RCA) report.     2.  Any new “Action Plan” milestones that were developed as a result of the third RCA report.     Thank you.      Patrick Monette-Shaw   Columnist/Reporter   Westside Observer Newspaper     cc:  Public Records Staff, SFDPH          Michaela Varisto         Zoe Harris

Pursuant to the California Public Records Act (Government Code § 7920 et seq.), I am requesting access to and copies of records related to FEMA Public Assistance (PA) projects administered by the City and County of San Francisco for the following disaster declarations:   DR-4482-CA (COVID-19 Pandemic, incident period January 20, 2020 – May 11, 2023)  DR-4683-CA (Severe Winter Storms, Flooding, Landslides, and Mudslides, incident period December 27, 2022 – January 31, 2023)  DR-4699-CA (Severe Winter Storms, Straight-line Winds, Flooding, Landslides, and Mudslides, incident period February 21, 2023 – July 10, 2023)   This request is submitted to the Controller's Office as the custodian of record for FEMA PA claims, per the direction of SF Public Works Custodian of Records David Steinberg (Request 26-2905, closed May 4, 2026).  I am requesting records in two tiers. Please prioritize Tier 1 in production. All categories in both tiers are within scope; none are withdrawn.  Tier 1 — Priority Production (Force Account Labor and Related Documentation)  1. Timesheets and time records. Per-employee, per-day time records for city employees whose labor costs were claimed under any of the three disaster declarations listed above. Includes: individual timesheet entries, time cards, electronic time export files (structured spreadsheet or system export preferred over scanned PDFs where available), and any timekeeper certification forms attached to payroll records.  2. Activity logs and crew logs. Daily records documenting the specific work performed by each employee during disaster response — including employee name, date, work location, and narrative description of the activity. Includes: ICS 214 forms, supervisor daily logs, crew activity sheets, site manager logs, and any equivalent record by any name used internally. Both handwritten and typed versions are requested.  3. Force Account Labor Summary documents. Aggregate roll-up reports by employee or pay period used to substantiate total labor costs claimed on a Project Worksheet. Includes: FEMA Form FF-104-FY-21-137 (Force Account Labor Summary Record) or equivalent, and any internally prepared labor cost workbooks submitted as supporting documentation.  4. Payroll records and certifications. Payroll registers, certified payroll records, pay stubs, and payroll system exports supporting the labor costs claimed. Fringe benefit rate schedules, fringe benefit calculations, and benefit component documentation (health, retirement, FICA, workers' compensation) attached to or submitted with any PA labor claim.  5. Overtime authorization forms. Pre-authorization records approving overtime work for employees whose overtime costs were claimed under any of the three declarations. Recommendation for San Francisco Public Works:  3.6 The Public Works Deputy Director of Operations, in coordination with the relevant IT departments, should modify the mobile application and/or software system used by Street Environmental Services (SES) field staff to make a time-stamped "completion photograph" a mandatory requirement for closing any 311 service request. The system must be configured to prevent a service request from being moved to a "completed" or "closed" status until at least one photograph has been successfully uploaded. This system enhancement should be fully implemented no later than March 31, 2026.  Benefits and Rationale:  A procedural policy requiring completion photos is a positive step, but a system-enforced requirement provides a much higher level of assurance and operational integrity. By hard-wiring this requirement into the technology crews use daily, the Department can guarantee compliance and eliminate ambiguity.  This system-enforced approach provides significant benefits:   Guaranteed Verification and Accountability: This change makes accountability systematic rather than just procedural. It creates a non-negotiable visual record for every completed task, ensuring that a request cannot be closed without evidence of completion. This provides an indisputable audit trail.  Enhanced Performance and Quality Assurance: A mandatory photo creates a reliable, real-time feedback loop. Supervisors are assured a visual of every job, allowing them to assess the quality of work consistently and efficiently without needing to conduct as many physical spot-checks.  Improved Operational Efficiency and Reduced Rework: By preventing premature or incomplete closures, this requirement reduces the likelihood that the same issue will be reported again, saving crew time and resources. It eliminates disputes over whether a task was completed and ensures that the initial response is sufficient.  Complete and Consistent Data: Mandating a photo for every closure ensures that the visual dataset of the Department's work is complete. This comprehensive data is invaluable for analyzing trends, demonstrating programmatic effectiveness to oversight bodies, and building public confidence.  Procedural Symmetry and Trust: If the public is asked to provide a photo to initiate a request, it is reasonable and fair for the Department to provide a photo to close it. This creates a closed-loop, evidence-based system that fosters transparency and trust between the city and its residents.   2. Revised Public Records Request (Targeting System Rules)  This request is now more specific, asking not just for policies but for the technical rules and configurations of the software itself. If unusual circumstances exist, any extension must be in writing from the head of the agency or a designee, must state the reasons, and may not exceed 14 days (§ 7922.535(b)–(c)). Production must then be made promptly (§ 7922.530(a)); § 7922.500 does not permit the agency to delay or obstruct inspection or copying. We know you normally post this information online, however that data does not seem to be appearing in a timely manner this year.  July 6th, 2026      We are requesting a copy of San Francisco's Employee Compensation Report for the 2025 calendar year under the provisions of California Gov. Code § 7920, the California Public Records Act.   The purpose of this request is to obtain records which provide a complete and comprehensive account of San Francisco's total costs associated with employee full names and compensation.   Specifically, this request seeks an accounting, by full name and job title, of total gross wages paid to each employee and the total cost incurred separately by the employer for providing retirement and health benefits.  Note that the State Controller’s “Government Compensation in California” report does not contain the names of employees and therefore does not satisfy this request. If your response is to send us a copy of that report, that will simply delay the process and take more of your time as we will reject it as insufficient to satisfy this request in full.  As a reminder, per Gov. Code § 7922.585(a)  “Nothing in this section is intended to affect the public record status of information merely because it is stored in a computer. Public records stored in a computer shall be disclosed as required by this chapter.”  In an effort to standardize how this information is reported, please include the following categories in your response:     Employee Name (full name, including first and last)  Position/Job Title (“City Manager”, “Police Officer”, etc.)  Annual Salary Minimum & Maximum   Total Regular Pay  Overtime Pay   Other Pay (any additional forms of pay that are not reported in Regular Pay)   Retirement Contribution Costs - All forms of employer-paid retirement contributions, deferred compensation, etc., including Unaccrued Actuarial Liability if applicable. Please split out per the standard State Controller’s Office categories.    Healthcare Contribution Costs - All forms of employer-paid health and welfare benefits, such as health, dental and vision insurance benefits.     In the event San Francisco is not in possession of a record of this nature, we request copies of any other record or records that contain information, even if only in part, that is responsive to the purpose of this request — employee name in conjunction with their compensation data for the period requested.  Please provide the requested materials or, per Gov. Code § 7922.535(a), a timeline along which they will be made available by, no later than ten days from the date of this request.   Per Gov. Code § 7922.570(a), we ask that you provide the records in an Excel spreadsheet format. You may provide this data to us by replying to this email and attaching your data file.  There is no need to password-protect your responsive data, that data will be posted to a publicly-available website when we’ve completed our review process.  Note that saving your original spreadsheet in the form of a PDF and sending that to us is not sufficient. Doing this will simply result in a need for you to take more time to respond, given that a PDF copy is not the original data, which is what we are requesting  As a reminder, Gov. Code § 7922.600(a) instructs public agencies to "assist requester in finding records and information that are responsive to the request or to the purpose of the request."  It is not necessary to prepare a boilerplate PDF response document sent to us as an attachment to email in order to respond with your ETA. We are well aware of the legal provisions of the CPRA, do not need them reiterated, and are happy to accept a simple response giving us the estimated date you will be able to provide the data requested.  If your response is to ask us to submit this request using a portal/request system, please note while we appreciate your use of such a system, pursuant to Gov. Code § 7922.535(a), public agencies are required to respond to any request for public records within 10 days of receipt. There is no statutory basis for requiring requesters submit a request in the agency's preferred format or medium, such as in person, on paper, or via an online portal.  Please feel free to contact us with any questions that you might have.  Thank you.  Municipalities Data Collections   Transparent California   muni@transparentcalifornia.com  Rev 4/20/2026

We’re attaching the S&P and Fitch reports for reference and can provide the following, attributable to the Controller’s Office, if you’d like to use it:     San Francisco is rated by three agencies — Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch — and each rating agency applies its own methodology and rating criteria. Thank you for your time and consideration,   Jenny Kwon  Graphics Reporter  The San Francisco Chronicle

Dear Records Custodian in the San Francisco Department of Public Health,    We are requesting access to the following records related to federal, state and local HIV funding:    Any financial documents related to Ending the HIV Epidemic (EHE), submitted between July 1, 2019, through June 30, 2023, to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.   Financial documents and/or funding reports for fiscal years 2021-22, 2022-23, and 2023-24 that detail the following:   Amount received in federal money for, excluding Ending the HIV Epidemic (EHE) funding, and amount spent on HIV prevention, testing and treatment efforts  Amount received in California money and amount spent on HIV prevention, testing and treatment efforts  Amount received in San Francisco County money and amount spent on HIV prevention, testing and treatment efforts   Any documents related to Ending the HIV Epidemic (EHE) reports, including but not limited to accomplishment and progress reports, submitted between July 1, 2019, through June 30, 2023, to a state or county agency that oversees EHE funding distribution.  Any financial documents, reports or communications that show how much of EHE funds went to organizations that serve Latinos and Hispanics in fiscal years 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24 for HIV prevention, testing and treatment.   Any financial documents or reports regarding federal Ryan White funding, either spending or distribution, in fiscal years 2021-22, 2022-23 and 2023-24, as well as, if possible:  The number of Latino and/or Hispanic patients who were served by Ryan White funding  The amount of money spent specifically on Latino and Hispanic populations or patients    We request the following information be provided in electronic format, if possible. Please waive any applicable fees, a request made in the disclosure that the information is in the public interest and will contribute significantly to the public’s understanding of public health funding for HIV prevention and treatment.   We are reporters with KFF Health News and The Associated Press, and this request is being sought for news-gathering purposes, not commercial purposes. If any fees are required, please contact me before proceeding with the processing of this request.    If possible, please provide responsive records in electronic form and on a rolling basis, as they become available.   The California Public Records Act (PRA) requires a response time of 10 business days. If access to the records will take longer, please contact us with more details about when we might expect to access the records. Also, please let us know if we can modify this request to better match your record-keeping and speed up this process.    If you deny or redact any or all of this request, please cite each specific exemption under the state’s public record laws you feel justifies the refusal to release the information and notify us of the appeal procedures available to me under the law.   Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.    Sincerely,    Vanessa G. Sánchez  407-76-8372   vanessas@kff.org   KFF Health News    Devna Bose  601-826-0644  dbose@ap.org  Associated Press

To whom it may concern,   Hi, my name is Jenny Kwon and I am a reporter with the San Francisco Chronicle. I am requesting the following records: Chat histories of all Microsoft CoPilot sessions conducted by city employees on city-owned devices or used in job-related functions.    The timeframe for this request is from July 14, 2025 through the date this request is processed.    This is a request for government agency records made under the right of access granted by the Constitution of the State of California as amended by the passage of Prop 59 on Nov. 3, 2004, as well as the provisions of the California Public Records Act, California Government Code §6251, with emphasis on the requirements of 6253.1. This request is dated Nov. 17, 2025. Please limit all communications about this request to email. Please do not telephone me about this matter.  I will also remind you that if portions of the information I have requested is exempt from disclosure by express provisions of law, government code section 6253 (a) additionally requires segregation and deletion of that material in order that the remainder of the information be released. If you determine that an express provision of law exists to exempt from disclosure all or a portion of the material I have requested, Government Code Section 6253(c) requires notification to me of the reasons for that determination. In addition, be advised that the Constitution of the State of California, as amended by Prop. 59, requires that you take the broadest possible position to disclose these records when reviewing this request. It is also your constitutional duty to take the narrowest possible view of any exemptions to the disclosure of these records. As you know, the act allows you 10 days to research this matter, collect responsive records, and issue determinations which, if any, of those records, are subject to narrow exemptions to disclosure. The 10-day period begins today, Nov. 17, 2025, the date this request was sent to you.   I also draw your attention to Government Code section 6253.1, which requires a public agency to assist the public in making a focused and effective request by (1) identifying records and information responsive to the request, (2) describing the information technology and physical location in which the records exist, and (3) providing suggestions for overcoming any practical basis for denying access to the records or information sought. Please provide your full compliance with 6253.1 should the need arise.   I also request a fee waiver for these records, as I am a representative of the news media as a graphics reporter for the San Francisco Chronicle. Thus, this request is made as part of news gathering and not for a commercial use. Disclosure of the requested information to me is in the public interest because it is likely to contribute to the public understanding of how local government is utilizing generative AI/AI models, and is not primarily in my commercial interest.  Additionally, please send these responsive records as they become available. In order to expedite this request, if there is a way to adjust the wording of this request to better match the way your record-keeping system generates reports, please let me know via email and I will gladly make an amendment.   I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 20 business days, as the statute requires. Thank you for your timely consideration of this request.  Thank you for your time and consideration,   Jenny Kwon  Graphics Reporter  The San Francisco Chronicle

Hi there,  I'm hoping to get more information about how San Francisco Public Works responds to 311 requests—specifically for things like illegal dumping, street and sidewalk cleaning, and graffiti removal. I'm trying to better understand the logistics, costs, and outcomes of these operations. I’d appreciate any data, documents, or resources you can provide related to the following:   How many employees are currently assigned to responding to 311 requests in the field  The number and types of vehicles used for these responses  Any standard operating procedures or internal guidance used to decide how and when to respond to a request  Average response time by category (e.g. illegal dumping, graffiti, encampments)  The number of 311 requests where staff arrived but didn’t take action (e.g. trash gone, not in scope, etc.)  The average or estimated cost to respond to a 311 request (ideally by category)  Annual or department-level budgets related to 311 response operations  Any performance metrics or evaluations used to assess 311-related work  Vehicle GPS or driving logs (if available), which could help clarify how trucks are deployed and routed  Any internal reporting or audits on the efficiency, cost-effectiveness, or outcomes of 311 request responses  Any financial statements that include breakdowns of spending on field operations, vehicle maintenance, or contractor use for 311 issues

This email provides the custodian list, forms of communication, and search terms you requested. It also responds to the Sunshine Team's email of today, which disclosed the search criteria used to date and addressed the Padilla text messages, because the two subjects belong together. Everything below concerns 248 Valley Street (Assessor Block 6614, Lot 015) and the adjacent property at 246 Valley Street. If it is easier to run this in phases, the first eight custodians are the priority.  1. (b) Text messages, SMS and MMS, and messages sent through any mobile messaging application, on Department issued devices or personal devices used for Department business. (e) Messages, chat, comments, and markup history within Bluebeam Studio, specifically Session 738-036-550 and Project 887-312-467.  3. Search terms, and why the prior criteria missed records  The Sunshine Team's email of today disclosed that the MIS search used eight spellings of the street address and no other terms. I appreciate the disclosure; it is the first time the Department has told me how a search was run, and it explains the results. Department staff do not always write out a street address when discussing a project. They refer to permit numbers, complaint numbers, and the parties. A search limited to address strings will, by design, miss every record that discusses this project by its numbers or its people without spelling the address.  For email and Teams, please search the following. Please treat permit, complaint, and reference numbers as matching whether written with or without periods, slashes, or spaces (for example 202212239051, 2022.1223.9051, 2022/1223/9051, and 2022 1223 9051 are the same permit).  Property: "248 Valley"; "246 Valley"; "248 A Valley"; "6614/015"; "Block 6614"  Permits and applications: 202212239051; 202510227848; PP20260407390; PM20260407392; 202604209756  Complaints: 202650384; 202650652; 202650659; 202652357; 202652745; 202653093; 202655751; 202657196; 202657744; 202658355; 202658780; 202659695; 202659696  Related references: 75038-1; 719670; ASB146438; CPM459609; CPM460412; A64989A; A64989B; 101003997738; 101003621234; 101003645390  Project parties: Quantix; "248 Valley LLC"; "A V Construction"; Abkowitz; DoubleD; doubledengineering.com; koengineering.com; Anton  Complainant: Beal; jeremy.reynolds.beal  4. Text messages and voicemail  Keyword searching is unreliable for text messages, so for form (b) and form (d) I suggest pulling by custodian and date range rather than by term, and then reviewing for the property. If it helps to narrow by counterparty, the numbers I know to be relevant are (757) 291-9198 (mine), (415) 812-5239 (248 Valley LLC per the Special Inspection form), and (650) 863-1674 (Quantix Real Estate Group per the same form).  5. Date ranges  For Joseph Chan, Stephen Liu, and any other plan review or permit processing staff: December 1, 2022 through the date the search is run, since the building permit application dates to late 2022.  For all other custodians: November 1, 2025 through the date the search is run, covering permit issuance and construction.  6. The Padilla text messages: the device and the account, not the employee  Today's email states that because Inspector Padilla is no longer with the Department, the Department is unable to obtain the text messages I requested. I note, and appreciate, that the Department does not dispute that these messages exist and are responsive. I hold copies of my side of the March 19, 2026 exchange with the Department's number (415) 646-1760.  The conclusion does not follow from the premise, for one reason: the messages were sent and received on a Department issued device, on a Department wireless account. The Department's ability to retrieve them does not depend on Inspector Padilla's employment status. It depends on what happened to the device and the account. So that we can resolve this rather than leave it at "unable to obtain," please answer the following, which overlap with the confirmations I requested from Director Kane on August 3:  (a) On what date did Inspector Padilla separate from the Department?  (b) Was the Department issued device assigned to him returned to the Department at separation? If yes, where is it now, and has it been wiped, reimaged, or reassigned, and if so on what date and by whom? If no, what steps has the Department taken to recover it?  (c) Does any backup, archive, or mobile device management system hold the contents of that device?  (d) The Department is the account holder on the wireless account serving (415) 646-1760. An account holder may obtain its own account records from its carrier without a subpoena. I am not asking the Department to seek message content from Verizon, and I understand the legal caution there. I ask that the Department promptly request from Verizon the call detail and message detail records for that line (date, time, direction, and counterparty number, not content) for November 1, 2025 through the line's deactivation, and that it also produce the billing statements and usage detail already in its files. I flag the timing because carriers typically retain message detail records for roughly one year, so delay itself will destroy this category.  (e) If the Department's position is that the contents of the device are destroyed or irretrievable, please state that expressly, together with the date of destruction and the authority under which it occurred. I would rather be told that plainly now than discover it later.  Today's email also states that text messages are not maintained by the Department. One question about that, for the record: is that a written policy, and if so may I have a copy? Administrative Code section 67.29-7 directs that correspondence and records be maintained and preserved, and a text message conducting Department business is a record regardless of the medium. I raise this so the Department's position on retention is stated clearly somewhere, not to argue it in this thread.  7. Prior requests for these records  So that the record is clear, this is not the first time these records have been requested. The chronology in brief:  On July 16, 2026, at 6:31 PM, I submitted a records request to dbi.sunshinerequests@sfgov.org whose scope included the March 19, 2026 text messages described above. The Department closed that request on July 27, 2026, without producing a single communication in any form.  On July 27, 2026, I sent a five item deficiency letter and raised the preservation and production of these categories as item 2. The Department's reply of July 28, 2026, at 8:34 AM, stated that it would reach out to the other divisions to review and respond.  On August 3, 2026, I delivered a preservation demand to Director Kane identifying these categories custodian by custodian.  Also on August 3, 2026, the Sunshine Team's response arrived. It disclosed the address-only search criteria described in section 3, and stated that the Padilla messages cannot be obtained because he has departed. The production that accompanied this process (NR26-6685) contained complaint data sheets and special inspection requirement forms, and no communications of any kind, even though the data sheets themselves record Department staff contacting the contractor and the building owners on at least four occasions.  This email is therefore the fifth time since July 16 that these records have been raised in writing. I do not say that to assign fault to your office, and I appreciate that you are the first person in this process to ask me for a custodian list, which is the right way to run the search. But that history is why the next section describes how I will verify what comes back.  8. Known records, and how I will verify completeness  I want to be transparent about how I will evaluate what comes back, because I think it will help the Department get this right the first time rather than in rounds.  From my own correspondence, from the Department's prior productions, and from third parties who have shared their correspondence with me, I maintain a reference set of records that I know to exist, organized by custodian and by form of communication. When records are produced, I will check the production against that set. By way of illustration and not limitation:  (a) The March 19, 2026 text exchange with Inspector Padilla described in section 6. I hold copies. A correctly executed search of form (b) for custodian 1 will return that exchange.  (b) I have corresponded by email with several of the custodians listed above, including my letter of July 23, 2026 to Director Kane. Each custodian's account should, at minimum, return the messages I sent to it. I hold the complete set of my own sent mail.  (c) A complete search must also return at least every internal Department email concerning this property that has already appeared in the Department's prior productions in this matter, since a new search of the same accounts cannot properly return less than an old one.  The reference set is larger than these examples, and I am deliberately not enumerating the rest of it. If a production comes back without records I know to exist, I will treat that as evidence that the search was not adequately executed rather than that the records do not exist, I will raise it formally, and I will pursue the remedies the Sunshine Ordinance provides, including a petition to the Supervisor of Records. I would much rather never need to write that letter, which is why I am describing the method now instead of invoking it later.  Two things will go a long way toward making that unnecessary. First, when the searches are complete, please tell me, for each custodian, which systems were searched, by whom, and whether the custodian responded. Second, if the Department concludes that a category of records does not exist or cannot be produced for a particular custodian, please say so expressly, per custodian and per category, rather than closing the request generally, so that any gap is visible while it is still easy to discuss and fix.  To be clear on scope, this email supplements and does not narrow my pending requests or the preservation demand delivered to Director Kane on August 3, which remains in effect, with its response date of Friday, August 7.  Thank you again for engaging with this constructively. I know this is long, and I have tried to order it so the most significant material comes first. Please confirm receipt, and let me know if a different format would be more useful or if I can narrow anything to make the first phase faster.

This was sent yesterday by email directly to Mr. Steinberg and Mr. Zarefsky in the Office of the City Attorney.  I got a reply from Mr. Steinberg, saying he is away and directing me to use this site:--   Gentlemen,   I set out here, for ease of reference by both you and the Office of the City Attorney, my recent Immediate Disclosure Request and your response. It will also provide for easy administrative and/or juridical review, if that proves necessary:  Immediate Disclosure Request  Please provide me with the complaint, inspection report, and any follow-up documents relating to the graffiti abatement notice at 930 Cole St. Please include any documents that identifies by name, not just initials, the abatement officer, the owner of the property to whom the notice was mailed, the complainant, the complaint itself, and a specification of what the graffiti is and where exactly it is, together with any intra- or inter- office communication relating to the notice. Please also provide the budget for graffiti abatement for the current fiscal year. Thank you very much.  Immediate Disclosure Request  (Emphasis supplied.)        Message to requester  We received your request, dated Nov. 2. You have requested the following records:     the complaint, inspection report, and any follow-up documents relating to the graffiti abatement notice at 930 Cole St.   the budget for graffiti abatement for the current fiscal year     Although you labeled your request as an Immediate Disclosure Request, it does not meet the requirement of an IDR as set forth in San Francisco Administrative Code Section 67.25(a). For this reason, we are treating this request as a standard public records request, subject to the normally applicable 10-day response time, with a possible extension. Accordingly, we will be in touch with you regarding the request by no later than Dec. 2.  Please see Pages 4-5 of the City Attorney's Opinion at https://sanfrancisco.nextrequest.com/documents/9556982/download for an explanation of the requirements for an Immediate Disclosure Request.  ….  Regards,  David A. Steinberg  Custodian of Records  San Francisco Public Works     You have cited the City Attorney's Memorandum, but failed to disclose how my request is not "simple, routine, or otherwise readily answerable". It concerns a single notice to abate graffiti on a single building with a known location. How can this be construed as not “simple, routine, or otherwise readily answerable"?  It cannot be sufficient to simply quote the City Department’s interpretation of the general law without some clear indication of how that interpretation relates to the facts of this request. I am entitled to know this.  Secondly, I am now making a “Nature of a Description Request." I want to know the existence, quantity, form, and nature of [your] department’s records” relating to this notice. You will note, of course, that you have seven days to respond. There are no extensions, as I take it you also know.  Finally, perhaps I need not say this, but I remind you of your department’s obligation to produce these records “as soon as reasonably possible on an incremental or single ‘rolling' basis, when so requested." I am so requesting, if you cannot give me what I assume will be relatively few documents.  We are aware that if this matter goes to court and I ultimately obtain the records, I shall recover only attorney’s fees and costs in the normal circumstances. However, the intentional withholding of records, or the intentional delaying of release of records, I submit -- if that is what is occurring here, I have no way of knowing this -- would be an entirely different matter with different possible outcomes. You will please forgive my mentioning this at this time, and perhaps it is unnecessary to do so.  I do not mean in any way to be contentious. But I do mean to obtain these records, as permitted by law, and not again be put off. I am also seeking to make it clear, in a memorialized way, that I am trying to preclude contentiousness and obtain what the freedom of information laws mandate.  In this honest effort, I would be grateful for the assistance of the City Attorney's Office. I hope that your action is not somehow in retaliation for an earlier piece I wrote for the Chronicle with regard to Public Works.  To state the obvious, we are dealing here with desperately important public rights to know what is being done by its government. As the Washington Post says daily, “Democracy Dies in the Dark.”  Aggravating your response, or failure to respond, to my simple request is your having redacted something—just a few words in a single entry, by the look of it -- in a response to my previous request. You listed a telephone book of potential grounds justifying redactions in general, but did not specify what ground you were relying on. Hence, you provided no ground at all. I pointed out to you at the time that you must provide this to assure that you have a lawful ground. You did not even respond. This gives rise to the issue of what the ground was, if you feel you have to not disclose it. I await an answer to that request as well. It is long overdue.  I look forward to the provision of the referenced information concerning the graffiti notice within one business day – that it, by the close of business tomorrow.   Thank you for your kind attention.   Sincerely,  Robert M. Smith

requests.request_text:
The purpose of this request is to obtain records, of which the San Francisco Department of Public Health (hereafter "SFDPH") may be custodian, that pertain to the ongoing project at the former Navy shipyard at Hunters Point (hereafter "shipyard"), including SFDPH preparation for the May 14 hearing related to the shipyard at the Board of Supervisors, as well as SFDPH communication with the US Environmental Protection Agency, US Navy, SF Mayor's Office, property developer at the shipyard, and members of the public. 
 Documents that may be responsive sought under this request include emails, memos, reports, meeting minutes, drafts, notes, and other material that pertains to the ongoing project at the shipyard. 
 The time frame for records sought under this request is January 20, 2018, to the present. 
   
 Please provide documents in electronic format. Please provide documents on a rolling basis as they become available. If any documents contain information subject to redaction, please provide redacted copies, with reasons for withholding this information cited, pursuant to the Sunshine Ordinance. 
 This request does not seek records that are already published online or otherwise readily available.  
   I make this request as an established journalist. This request concerns a major development project, an ongoing scandal that has resulted in federal criminal charges and is of the utmost interest to the public, including the occupants of 300 units of occupied housing at The SF Shipyard. For these reasons, this request is not unduly burdensome. I urge you to consider these factors when responding to this request.

Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, Section 6250 et seq. of the Government Code and the California state Constitution, as amended by Proposition 59, and section 13300 of the California Penal Code, I am asking for the records of all personal property collected and logged during encampment resolutions or cleanings in the years 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2022 in the city of San Francisco and stored by the Department of Public Works or another city agency at the Public Works Operations Yard (2323 Cesar Chavez St) or other storage locations.    Specifically, I am requesting the following data fields for each case (if applicable):   date and time belonging(s) were collected, location belonging(s) were collected from, name and contact information of owner of belonging(s), description of belonging(s), Public Works staff name, Public Works staff supervisor name, San Francisco Police Department officer name, and San Francisco Police Department badge number, the status of the items (returned to owner, discarded, pending, etc). Additionally, I’m requesting any record of the belongings disposed of at each cleanup, including the amount of trash processed during the cleanup. Please provide this in an excel or other machine readable format if possible.   I am also requesting any photos taken during the cleaning by city staff, including photos of tents that are going to be discarded, pictures of the encampments before/after cleaning, and/or images of property that was collected and stored.   Lastly, I am requesting data on the number of encampment cleanings and resolutions that occurred each month during the last 5 years (2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, and 2023 through the date of this request).   I am making this request as a journalist conducting research into homeless encampment cleanups. I believe that the release of this information would help enhance the public’s understanding of how encampments are cleaned and the impact of that on residents and neighborhoods.   This request reasonably describes identifiable information that the California Public Records Act requires be made public. Accordingly, I ask that you make the records promptly available.    In case there are problems with my request, the Public Records Act requires government agencies to assist members of the public to identify records and information responsive to the request, describe the information technology in which the records exist and to provide suggestions for overcoming any practical basis for denying access to the records or information sought.   To the extent that a portion of the information I have requested is exempt by express provisions of law, the public records act additionally requires segregation and deletion of that material in order that the remainder of the information may be provided in satisfaction of my request.   If you determine that an express provision of law exists to exempt from disclosure all or a portion of the material I have requested, the Public Records Act requires a determination and notification to me of the reasons no later than 10 days from your receipt of this request. The act prohibits the use of the 10-day period, or any provision of the act, “to delay access for purposes of inspecting public records.”   Please notify me in advance of any estimate of costs to produce the records in fulfillment of this request. If you have any questions, please email me at ruth.talbot@propublica.org.   Thank you for your time!

To whom it may concern,   Hi, my name is Jenny Kwon and I am a reporter with the San Francisco Chronicle. I am requesting the following records: Chat histories of all Microsoft CoPilot sessions conducted by city employees on city-owned devices or used in job-related functions.    The timeframe for this request is from July 14, 2025 through the date this request is processed.    This is a request for government agency records made under the right of access granted by the Constitution of the State of California as amended by the passage of Prop 59 on Nov. 3, 2004, as well as the provisions of the California Public Records Act, California Government Code §6251, with emphasis on the requirements of 6253.1. This request is dated Nov. 17, 2025. Please limit all communications about this request to email. Please do not telephone me about this matter.  I will also remind you that if portions of the information I have requested is exempt from disclosure by express provisions of law, government code section 6253 (a) additionally requires segregation and deletion of that material in order that the remainder of the information be released. If you determine that an express provision of law exists to exempt from disclosure all or a portion of the material I have requested, Government Code Section 6253(c) requires notification to me of the reasons for that determination. In addition, be advised that the Constitution of the State of California, as amended by Prop. 59, requires that you take the broadest possible position to disclose these records when reviewing this request. It is also your constitutional duty to take the narrowest possible view of any exemptions to the disclosure of these records. As you know, the act allows you 10 days to research this matter, collect responsive records, and issue determinations which, if any, of those records, are subject to narrow exemptions to disclosure. The 10-day period begins today, Nov. 17, 2025, the date this request was sent to you.   I also draw your attention to Government Code section 6253.1, which requires a public agency to assist the public in making a focused and effective request by (1) identifying records and information responsive to the request, (2) describing the information technology and physical location in which the records exist, and (3) providing suggestions for overcoming any practical basis for denying access to the records or information sought. Please provide your full compliance with 6253.1 should the need arise.   I also request a fee waiver for these records, as I am a representative of the news media as a graphics reporter for the San Francisco Chronicle. Thus, this request is made as part of news gathering and not for a commercial use. Disclosure of the requested information to me is in the public interest because it is likely to contribute to the public understanding of how local government is utilizing generative AI/AI models, and is not primarily in my commercial interest.  Additionally, please send these responsive records as they become available. In order to expedite this request, if there is a way to adjust the wording of this request to better match the way your record-keeping system generates reports, please let me know via email and I will gladly make an amendment.   I look forward to receiving your response to this request within 20 business days, as the statute requires. Thank you for your timely consideration of this request.  Thank you for your time and consideration,   Jenny Kwon  Graphics Reporter  The San Francisco Chronicle

Hello Public Records Officer,  Pursuant to the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.) and the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance, I request copies of records that describe and govern how the City paints, maintains, and removes graffiti from fire call boxes / “fire boxes,” including any boxes treated as “historic” or otherwise excluded from routine painting.  This request is prompted by ongoing graffiti/paint deterioration concerns described in SolveSF report #101003579292: https://solvesf.com/report/101003579292  Records requested (please produce for 2018–present unless otherwise noted)  A) Policies, SOPs, and standards   Any written policies, standard operating procedures (SOPs), work instructions, style guides, or specifications covering:  Painting fire boxes (including color standards, coatings, surface prep, curing times, and quality checks)  Graffiti removal/abatement on fire boxes (approved solvents/cleaners, pressure washing guidance, repaint triggers)  Special handling for “historic,” “heritage,” or “landmark” boxes (including required approvals, restrictions, or materials)    Any criteria or decision documents defining what makes a fire box “historic” (or otherwise treated differently), including:  Lists/inventories of “historic” fire boxes  Any internal guidance or external requirements (e.g., preservation requirements) that affect repainting or graffiti removal     B) Work assignment and responsibility   Records identifying which department(s), division(s), shop(s), or contractors are responsible for:  Routine painting of fire boxes  Graffiti abatement on fire boxes  Responding to 311/SolveSF tickets about fire boxes    Any documents explaining why the work is assigned to a specific shop/unit (and not delegated to another City paint shop or vendor) including:  Memos, emails, decision notes, or management directives about assignment, workload, prioritization, or limitations  Any risk/safety rationale (e.g., electrical/communications constraints, access requirements)     C) Contracts, scopes, and funding (if applicable)   If any painting/graffiti work is contracted out (in whole or part), please provide:  Contracts, scopes of work, task orders, pricing sheets, SLAs/response-time requirements, and amendments  Any vendor performance metrics or reports related to fire box painting or graffiti abatement    Budget/funding records that relate specifically to painting/graffiti abatement for fire boxes, including:  Budget line items, internal service orders, cost codes, or funding allocations  Any documents describing backlog, staffing constraints, or prioritization due to funding     D) Operational records for the reported location(s)   For the fire box(es) implicated by SolveSF report #101003579292 (and any internal asset IDs tied to that report), please provide:  Work orders, inspection notes, service logs, completion photos, and materials used  Communications (emails/msgs) about whether/when it would be repainted or cleaned, and why/why not  Any records showing ticket routing between departments/shops/contractors     Format, search, and processing   Please provide records electronically (PDF preferred; spreadsheets in native format such as .xlsx/.csv).  Please include responsive emails in .pst/.mbox or PDF, with attachments preserved.  If any portion is exempt, please produce all segregable portions and provide an index of withheld records describing the legal basis for each withholding (including the specific exemption(s) relied upon). This request is to the San Francisco Weights and Measures Program run by the SFDPH. I would like to obtain information regarding San Francisco’s price accuracy/price verification inspections of supermarket/grocery and other retail stores over time.    I would like as follows:   *A brief description of the program including whether inspections are regularly undertaken as part of a program, or if they are only undertaken in response to consumer complaints; a breakdown of the types of stores included in the program (eg supermarket/grocery, convenience, drug/pharmacy, clothing etc); and the procedure if overcharges/undercharges are found (are stores notified?) and whether/when this would escalate to them being issued with a fine or notice of violation.  *Whether any error rate cut off is used in issuing alerts or violations, and what it is.   Then I would like to obtain the following data for each of the following years (mirroring the annual reporting periods used in the California Department of Food and Agriculture Division of Measurement Standards fiscal year expenditure reports which amalgamate data submitted annually by each county weights and measures section).   Years:  *2023/24 (which would cover data from 07/01/23 to 06/30/24)   *2022/23 (which would cover data from 07/01/22 to 06/30/23)   *2021/22 (which would cover data from 07/01/21 to 06/30/22)  *2020/21 (which would cover data from 07/012/20 to 06/30/21)  *2019/20 (which would cover data from 07/01/19 to 06/30/20)  *2018/19 (which would cover data from 07/01/18 to 06/30/19)  *2017/18 (which would cover data from 07/01/17 to 06/30/18)  *Any more years you are able to provide data for easily   I would like the following data for each of the above years (data provided by year):  *Total number of registered stores/businesses with point-of-sale systems  *Total number of price accuracy/price verification inspections  *Total number of locations (unique stores/businesses) at which price accuracy/price verification inspections were performed.  *Total number of inspections with overcharges  *Total number of inspections with undercharges  *Total number of locations with overcharges   *Total number of locations with undercharges  *Total number of items checked for price accuracy  *Total number of items with overcharges  *Total number of items without undercharges  *Total number of alerts/notifications issued to stores regarding overcharge/undercharge   *Total number of notices of violation issued to stores regarding overcharge/undercharge   *Total number of locations alerted/notified regarding undercharge/overcharge  *Total number of locations issued with a notice of violation regarding overcharge/undercharge   *Number of locations with more than one notice of violation issued  *Total number of consumer complaints in the period related to price verification/overcharging/undercharging  *Total hours dedicated to price accuracy/price verification inspections    I am keen to get the data asap, but I realize I am asking for a number of years of data here. If you were able to provide data for 2023/24 and 2022/23 in the first instance, I would be very grateful. I would like to receive the data in the form of an electronic excel spreadsheet or pdf.    I am deeply appreciative of the time that weights and measures staff have taken in broadly explaining the San Francisco price verification program. Please reach out if issues arise, there is something I have missed or am not understanding correctly, or you would like more information from me - for example please feel free to reach out if I need to simplify the request.   email: zoe@zoecorbyn.com  Cell: 415 413 6976  Landline: 415 683 7280
