Subject: Public Records Request — AI Chatbot Interaction Logs  April 9, 2026  Public Records Officer  San Francisco Department of Technology  One South Van Ness Avenue, 2nd Floor  San Francisco, CA 94103  Dear Public Records Officer,  I am writing on behalf of a team of researchers and journalists from Stanford University, the University of Southern California, KNKX Public Radio and the New York Times. We are studying how government agencies are adopting and using AI tools in their daily work.  We are writing to request records related to San Francisco's use of generative AI tools by city employees.  We are requesting the following records:  1. All interaction logs from Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, ChatGPT, or any other generative AI chatbot tool — including prompts submitted by city employees and responses generated by the AI — for the period from April 1, 2025 through the date this request is processed. We request these records in their native electronic format where available (e.g., HTML exports, JSON, or CSV).  2. Any policies, guidelines, acceptable use policies, or training materials governing city employee use of Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, ChatGPT, or other generative AI chatbot tools.  3. Any data retention or deletion policies applicable to AI chatbot interaction logs, including any schedules for automatic deletion of interaction data.  4. Administrative usage statistics for Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat and any other generative AI chatbot tools showing number of users, sessions, and queries processed.  We are seeking the substantive content of AI interactions for research purposes. We do not need personally identifying information of individual employees (such as names and email addresses).  On July 14, 2025, Mayor Daniel Lurie announced that Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, powered by OpenAI's GPT-4o, would be made available to nearly 30,000 city employees, making San Francisco the largest U.S. city to offer generative AI to its entire workforce (see CNBC, "San Francisco rolls out Microsoft's Copilot AI for 30,000 city workers," July 14, 2025, https://www.cnbc.com/2025/07/14/san-francisco-ai.html; see also SF.gov, "Mayor Lurie Brings AI Technology to San Francisco Government," https://www.sf.gov/news-mayor-lurie-brings-ai-technology-to-san-francisco-government-cementing-city-as-global-ai-leader). The rollout followed a successful six-month AI pilot in which more than 2,000 city employees tested generative AI tools and reported productivity gains of up to five hours per week (see GovTech, "San Francisco Gives Thousands of City Staffers AI Access," https://www.govtech.com/artificial-intelligence/san-francisco-gives-thousands-of-city-staffers-ai-access). The Department of Technology launched a five-week training program with live workshops and office hours for Copilot Chat.  We note that records of this type have been made available in response to public records requests in other jurisdictions. See Cascade PBS, WA City Officials Are Using ChatGPT to Write Government Documents (Aug. 2025), https://www.cascadepbs.org/news/2025/08/wa-city-officials-are-using-chatgpt-to-write-government-documents/; see also Texas State AI Usage — Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT), MuckRock, https://www.muckrock.com/foi/texas-109/texas-state-ai-usage-texas-department-of-transportation-txdot-196227/#files.  The results of this research will be published in peer-reviewed academic venues and will contribute to public understanding of how public servants interact with AI systems. This request is made by an academic research institution for scholarly, non-commercial purposes; as such, we request a fee waiver or reduction. If a fee waiver is not granted, please inform me of estimated costs before proceeding. I am willing to pay fees up to $20.  I understand that this may be a novel type of records request and I am happy to answer any technical questions. Please feel free to contact me at the email address or phone number below.  Thank you for your time and assistance.  Sincerely,  Alexander Spangher  Postdoctoral Researcher  Stanford University  alexspan@stanford.edu  P.S. To facilitate your response, we note that for Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat, interaction histories may be available through the Microsoft 365 admin console or the Purview compliance center. ChatGPT conversation histories can be exported by individual users via Settings > Data Controls > Export Data. Given the scale of the Copilot Chat deployment (30,000 employees), Microsoft's enterprise administrative tools should enable bulk export of interaction data. We are happy to provide additional technical guidance if that would be helpful.  P.P.S. Under the California Public Records Act, Cal. Gov. Code 6253(c), and the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance, public records include "any writing containing information relating to the conduct of the public's business prepared, owned, used, or retained by any state or local agency regardless of physical form or characteristics." Cal. Gov. Code 6252(e). AI chatbot interaction logs created or used by city employees in the course of their official duties qualify as public records under this definition. The city's official announcement of the Copilot Chat rollout to all 30,000 employees confirms these tools are part of the conduct of public business. Additionally, NARA Bulletin 2023-02 (Jan. 5, 2023), https://www.archives.gov/records-mgmt/bulletins/2023/2023-02, provides persuasive authority that chats and electronic messages used for government business are likely government records. The White House.: https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/speeches-remarks/2024/10/25/remarks-by-president-biden-on-the-biden-harris-administrations-record-of-delivering-for-tribal-communities-including-keeping-his-promise-to-make-this-historic-visit-to-indian-country-lavee/           [x] Alex White Plume, 73, a former president of the Oglala Sioux Tribe who attended two boarding schools on reservations in South Dakota, told NBC News he would not accept the apology from the president. “I don’t really see any way where we could accept it, because it doesn’t change anything,” White Plume said. “We need to survive, and in order to survive we need our territories back so we could bring back our language and perform the ceremonies that are specific to places in our territory," he said. "So I don’t want to accept an apology. I want them to be meaningful. And if it’s a meaningful apology, he would say, 'Okay, we’re gonna investigate the genocide, and we’ll establish a process to create protocols on how to go about it.' I think something like that would have been more meaningful.”      Cecelia Fire Thunder, 78, who became the first female president of the Oglala Sioux Tribe, and her three sisters attended Holy Rosary Mission School in 1953, now known as Red Cloud Indian School, on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. She said an "apology is about making sure that our community is receiving resources for behavioral health if there’s a trickle down effect of what happened 50 or 60 years ago." "There is no word for forgiveness in our language," she added. "Just because you acknowledge somebody hurt you, and you say, ‘I forgive you,’ that doesn’t mean the pain left; the pain is still there." Fire Thunder said an apology "should open the door for people to ask the question, ‘What happened?’ It should open the door not just for Native people, but for all of America, because they don’t know."      Marsha Small, a 65-year-old specialist in ground-penetrating radar, led the search in 2022 for unmarked graves for children who died while attending Red Cloud Indian School. “I’m a little angry,” she said. “But I’m appreciative of President Biden acknowledging this.” “In their statement, the White House says we must learn from that history so that’s never repeated,” Small added. “Well, we’re still living the nightmare. January 16, 2025    City and County of San Francisco        Re:     Public Records Request Pursuant to California Gov’t Code § 7920.000 et seq.   To the PRA Records Coordinator,   Please find below a formal request under the California Public Records Act (“CPRA”) and the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance for access to certain public records in the possession of the City and County of San Francisco.   Pursuant to the CPRA, we request that you make available all public records in your possession as described in the “Records Requested” section below. Gov’t. Code § 7920.000 et seq. We ask that you provide your response within 10 days, either by providing all the requested records or by providing a written response stating when the records will be made available and setting forth the legal authority for withholding or redacting any records. Gov’t. Code §§ 7922.000, 7922.535, 7922.540.    In making this request, it is our hope to place as little burden as possible on you and your staff. Please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any questions or if there are alternative ways of securing the same records requested herein.   Definitions Used in this Request:    “Communication” or “communications” means any form or transmittal of information from one person or organization to another that results in the creation of a document, including but not limited to letters, memoranda, notes, emails, electronic messages, text messages, social media messages or posts, contracts, agreements, and facsimile transmissions.   “Document” or “documents” is used in its broadest sense and includes all writings of any kind (in physical and/or electronically stored form), including, but not limited to, books, records, letters, telegrams, memoranda, electronic mail, instant messages, online chat messages (including but not limited to, Google Hangouts, iMessage, iChat, Jabber, WhatsApp, WeChat, Viber, Slack), voice-mail messages, reports, studies, speeches, calendars or diary entries, minutes, pamphlets, handwritten notes, drafts, charts, tabulations, data compilations, photographs, audiotapes and/or videotapes of conferences, and telephone or other conversations or communications in the City and County of San Francisco’s actual or constructive possession, custody, or control.   The term also includes reproductions or film impressions of any of the aforementioned writings, tape recordings, documents stored on computer hard disks, removable disks, tape back-up, or in any computer or electronic information storage device, any form of communication or representation, including letters, words, pictures, sounds, or symbols, or combinations thereof, and including all tangible printouts of information stored in any computer, word processor, server, internet, or electronic information storage device, including printouts of e-mails, and copies of documents which are not identical duplicates of the originals, and copies of all documents of which the originals are not in the City and County of San Francisco’s possession, custody, or control.    Separate Requests Requiring Separate Responses:   Subject to the above definitions, the records we request are specified below. Please treat each subparagraph below as a separate request under the CPRA and respond to each separately as to: (1) the existence of such records; (2) whether you intend to make such records available; (3) if you claim any exemption or privilege, and how that privilege applies; and (4) an estimate of when records will be produced or made available. This procedure is intended to avoid the waste of sending separate requests for each category of records. Unless we hear otherwise from you, we will assume that sending separate requests will not be necessary.   Records Requested:    Pursuant to the CPRA, please provide the records described below:    All street maintenance records pertaining to Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue;  All claims complaining received concerning the sidewalk between Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;  All documents that reflect your insurance coverage related to Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue;   All contracts and subcontracts for construction, roadwork, improvements, or other projects for work that includes work in the area of Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;   All 311 requests made to the City and County of San Francisco in the area of Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;   All photos attached to 311 requests made to the City and County of San Francisco in the area of Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;   All notes, reports, memorandums, emails, or other writings arising from the Department of Public Works employees visits to Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue;   All invoices related to repairs, construction, roadwork, improvements or other projects to Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue;   All writings that incidents resulting in injuries that involve pedestrians on Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue, for the last five (5) years;   List of all lawsuits, settlement demands, and complaints that arise from collisions, incidents, and events resulting in injury that occurred in the area of Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for last five (5) years;   All complaints you have received concerning Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;    All documents related to work that was performed, supervised, or contracted for, by the City of San Francisco, or any of its agencies, on Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;  All documents related to inspections that were performed, supervised, or contracted for, by the City of San Francisco, or any of its agencies, on Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue for the last five (5) years;  All documents related to any street inspection programs for the City of San Francisco, or any of its agencies, that have been in place at any time for the last five (5) years;  All documents related to any street construction, maintenance, and/or repair standards and/or guidelines that have been in place for the City of San Francico, or any of its agencies, at any time for the last five (5) years;  The Code for Safe Practices used by the City of San Francisco, or any of its agencies, for street and sidewalk maintenance, repairs, and/or pothole repairs;  All street survey guidelines, instructions, templates, and/or forms, that have been in place and/or used by the City of San Francisco, or any of its agencies, at any time for the last five (5) years;  All street survey templates and/or forms pertaining to Lake Street between Arguello Boulevard Avenue and 6th Avenue that were filled out by the City of San Francisco, or any of its agencies, at any time for the last five (5) years    Claims of Exemption:   If the City and County of San Francisco determines that any of the information requested is exempt from disclosure under the CPRA, please provide a statement in writing as to the legal basis of the exemption, including whether the exception is discretionary and, if so, why it is necessary to exercise discretion to withhold such information. Gov’t. Code §§ 7922.000, 7922.540. If the City and County of San Francisco determines that some, but not all, of the information is exempt from disclosure and you intend to withhold it, please redact those portions deemed exempt and provide the rest. Gov’t. Code § 7922.525.  Scope of Request:  This request applies to all relevant records in the possession of the City and County of San Francisco and includes documents that were created by a member of another government agency or a member of the public. See California State University v. Superior Court, 90 Cal.App.4th 810, 824-25 (1999). Please provide entire documents, even if only parts of them are responsive to this request.   Request for Assistance:   We have made a good faith effort to describe the records that we seek and further request your assistance to identify any and all records related to the purpose of our request but not specifically described herein. Please note that the CPRA allows a member of the public to request records by describing their content, rather than asking for specific documents by name; an agency that receives such a request must “search for records based on criteria set forth in the search request.” California First Amendment Coalition v. All records reflecting approval of the design, installation, or modification of any bike lane, bikeway, median, island, curb, or traffic control device at the Location. This includes San Francisco Public Works  Board of Directors resolutions, calendar items, staff reports, and minutes; Engineering Public Hearing notices, agendas, and results; Transportation Advisory Staff Committee (TASC) records; and signed engineering approvals.  2. Alternative design criteria. All records concerning the use or adoption, for any bikeway at the Location, of minimum safety design criteria other than those established by Caltrans, under Streets and Highways Code § 891(b). All plans, design memoranda, analyses, and communications concerning how eastbound bicyclists are directed from Page Street into and along Market Street. This includes:     channelization, lane-line, and conflict-marking plans for the Market/Page/Franklin intersection;  analyses of bicyclist travel paths, turning movements, or sight distance to the median(s) from the Page Street approach;  any evaluation of whether bicyclists entering Market Street from Page Street may conflict with the median(s).     5. Signal timing. Signal timing plans, phasing diagrams, and bicycle signal records for the Market/Page/Franklin and Market/12th Street intersections, including all changes and their dates.  6. Page Street bikeway projects. All approval, design, and evaluation records for bicycle facilities on eastbound Page Street between Octavia Boulevard and Market Street. Collisions and safety analyses. All records of collisions or incidents at the Location involving bicyclists, including collisions with curbs, medians, or islands, and including incidents involving riders traveling from Page Street onto Market Street. As another reminder, I am informed by Epic Corporation that Epic's standard "enterprise" package contains a "Patient Flow" module that contains the location patients are discharged to — including the name and type of facility; and the facility's street address, name of the City/Town, state, and zip code — in its "Case Management Discharge" feature.  Finally, as a reminder, there is only one City (San Francisco) in the County of San Francisco. Therefore, a database query against the name of Cities patients have been discharged to that do not equal "San Francisco" would identify and yield patients who were, in fact, discharged out-of-county. [I wrote such ad hoc database queries when I helped develop over a decade LHH's Microsoft Access "Rehabilitation Database" that tracked, in part, patient discharge dispositions.]     Please provide any and all e-mails and phone records between Ms. Vien and any and all other SFDPH employees in which Ms. Vien was informed that Epic does not track out-of-county discharges. We are building a resource to help small food businesses in California find safe, compliant, permitted kitchen facilities, and we would like to include San Francisco County in that directory. A PDF export or a link to a published dataset or online portal works equally well. If these records are already publicly available online, simply pointing us to that resource is sufficient and we will not need anything further from your office. Clarification   If any part of this request is unclear or would be easier to fulfill in a narrower form, please don't hesitate to reach out. We are happy to adjust the scope, complete any required forms, or provide additional information about our organization.   Thank you sincerely for your time and for your department's work in maintaining these records.

Citing court documents, Variety reported that the actress – referred in the suit as Jane Doe – alleged that Weinstein “forcibly performed oral sex on her, repeatedly masturbated in front of her and threatened to harm her career if she objected.” “I slept with Jennifer Lawrence and look where she is; she has just won an Oscar,” the accuser recalled Weinstein telling her, Variety reported.       In a statement obtained by People, Lawrence – who won an Oscar for the Weinstein produced film Silver Linings Playbook – denied any sexual relationship with Weinstein.       “My heart breaks for all the women who were victimized by Harvey Weinstein,” Lawrence 28, said. “I have never had anything but a professional relationship with him. People.: https://people.com/movies/jennifer-lawrence-denies-harvey-weinstein-alleged-brag-sexual-relationship/     [xii] Eventually, Lawrence realized that too many people were involved in making the decisions that should have been hers alone, and in August 2018, as she wrapped reshoots for the “X-Men” film “Dark Phoenix,” she left CAA, the agency that represented her for 10 years. “I had let myself be hijacked,” she said.  Lawrence has always had a gift for candor: Onscreen, she’ll show you things — and offscreen, tell you things — that other actresses, fortified by fame, tend to keep at a remove. Maybe she never had time to develop a protective shell. When “Winter’s Bone” was released, Lawrence was only 19; a year later, she was cast as Katniss Everdeen in “The Hunger Games,” and only two years after that, she won an Oscar for “Silver Linings Playbook.” “Jennifer Lawrence is Katniss Everdeen, I guess,” Jennifer Lawrence said. “Is that weird?” Who is Jennifer Lawrence Now? The New York Times.: https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/02/movies/jennifer-lawrence-causeway.html      [xiii] Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence is gearing up for a more significant presence behind the camera with the launch of production company Excellent Cadaver. With her producing partner Justine Polsky, Lawrence and Excellent Cadaver have inked a first-look film deal with Brad Weston’s Makeready. Under the agreement, Makeready will have a first look at the film projects Excellent Cadaver develops and produces. Through the first-look film deal, Makeready and Excellent Cadaver will finance and produce films both independently and as part of Makeready’s deals with Universal and Entertainment One. The deal encompasses films that Lawrence and Polsky will produce, and some that Lawrence will additionally star in. Makeready’s head of film, Pam Abdy, will oversee any Excellent Cadaver projects.           “In a relatively short amount of time, Jennifer has already proven herself to be a one-of-a-kind actress and businesswoman,” says Weston. “Her versatility and commitment to working with the greatest filmmakers in the industry highlights our shared ambition to create thoughtful, fearless films, and we are extremely excited to partner with Jennifer and Justine as they start this new chapter.” “Brad and Pam are visionary producers with incredible taste and a history of supporting diverse and compelling storytelling. We are thrilled to be partnering with Makeready and look forward to this exciting collaboration,” added Lawrence and Polsky. Weston, the former president and CEO of New Regency, launched Makeready in 2017 with backing from eOne and a five-year agreement with Uni to handle worldwide distribution and marketing on two feature films per year. The company is currently developing Queen & Slim, the debut feature for Emmy winner Lena Waithe starring Get Out actor Daniel Kaluuya. Jennifer Larence Launches Production Company Excellent Cadaver. The Hollywood Reporter.: https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/jennifer-lawrence-launches-production-company-excellent-cadaver-1156266/   Such is the cannibalistic nature of the Hollywood starlet cycle: when a female star is on the rise, our culture is all too happy to chew her up and spit her back out, deeming her “annoying” for all the reasons we previously enjoyed her. It happened to Anne Hathaway, and it also affected Jennifer Lawrence, who admitted during an event at the BFI London Film Festival that she “lost a sense of control” during the peak of her fame. “Between the Hunger Games coming out and winning the Oscar, I became such a commodity that I felt like every decision was a big, big group decision,” she said (per Deadline). “Because I had no idea what a huge movie star does next or what Katniss Everdeen should do after this… When I reflect now, I think of those following years as just kind of a loss of control and then a reaction to try to get back.”      The actor has returned to indie filmmaking with her new movie Causeway, the first project she’s produced under her company Excellent Cadaver. She explained the name during the event: “It’s a Sicilian mafia term for a hit on a major celebrity. It just made sense. I think there was a part of me that wanted to execute that part of me.”And there has been, if not a death per se, a closing of a chapter for Lawrence. While she was once the queen of the blockbuster—headlining The Hunger Games as well as the X-Men reboot series—those days are now, apparently, over. “Franchises are so fun. … I could never do one now cause I’m just too old and brittle,” the 32-year-old told the crowd. Instead, she’s setting a new course. “I’m so happy that I eventually, finally, in my late 20s kind of just stopped and made some major changes, and I got the voice in my head back,” Lawrence reflected. “Now, it feels personal to me for the first time in a long time.” Jennifer Lawrence knows things got a bit weird there for a minute. When “Winter’s Bone” was released, Lawrence was only 19; a year later, she was cast as Katniss Everdeen in “The Hunger Games,” and only two years after that, she won an Oscar for “Silver Linings Playbook.” “Jennifer Lawrence is Katniss Everdeen, I guess,” Jennifer Lawrence said. “Is that weird?” Who is Jennifer Lawrence Now? The New York Times.: https://www.nytimes.com/2022/11/02/movies/jennifer-lawrence-causeway.html      [xiii] Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence is gearing up for a more significant presence behind the camera with the launch of production company Excellent Cadaver. With her producing partner Justine Polsky, Lawrence and Excellent Cadaver have inked a first-look film deal with Brad Weston’s Makeready. Under the agreement, Makeready will have a first look at the film projects Excellent Cadaver develops and produces. Through the first-look film deal, Makeready and Excellent Cadaver will finance and produce films both independently and as part of Makeready’s deals with Universal and Entertainment One. The deal encompasses films that Lawrence and Polsky will produce, and some that Lawrence will additionally star in. Makeready’s head of film, Pam Abdy, will oversee any Excellent Cadaver projects.           “In a relatively short amount of time, Jennifer has already proven herself to be a one-of-a-kind actress and businesswoman,” says Weston. “Her versatility and commitment to working with the greatest filmmakers in the industry highlights our shared ambition to create thoughtful, fearless films, and we are extremely excited to partner with Jennifer and Justine as they start this new chapter.” “Brad and Pam are visionary producers with incredible taste and a history of supporting diverse and compelling storytelling. We are thrilled to be partnering with Makeready and look forward to this exciting collaboration,” added Lawrence and Polsky. Weston, the former president and CEO of New Regency, launched Makeready in 2017 with backing from eOne and a five-year agreement with Uni to handle worldwide distribution and marketing on two feature films per year. The company is currently developing Queen & Slim, the debut feature for Emmy winner Lena Waithe starring Get Out actor Daniel Kaluuya. Jennifer Larence Launches Production Company Excellent Cadaver. The Hollywood Reporter.: https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/jennifer-lawrence-launches-production-company-excellent-cadaver-1156266/   Such is the cannibalistic nature of the Hollywood starlet cycle: when a female star is on the rise, our culture is all too happy to chew her up and spit her back out, deeming her “annoying” for all the reasons we previously enjoyed her. It happened to Anne Hathaway, and it also affected Jennifer Lawrence, who admitted during an event at the BFI London Film Festival that she “lost a sense of control” during the peak of her fame. “Between the Hunger Games coming out and winning the Oscar, I became such a commodity that I felt like every decision was a big, big group decision,” she said (per Deadline). “Because I had no idea what a huge movie star does next or what Katniss Everdeen should do after this… When I reflect now, I think of those following years as just kind of a loss of control and then a reaction to try to get back.”      The actor has returned to indie filmmaking with her new movie Causeway, the first project she’s produced under her company Excellent Cadaver. She explained the name during the event: “It’s a Sicilian mafia term for a hit on a major celebrity. It just made sense. I think there was a part of me that wanted to execute that part of me.”And there has been, if not a death per se, a closing of a chapter for Lawrence. While she was once the queen of the blockbuster—headlining The Hunger Games as well as the X-Men reboot series—those days are now, apparently, over. “Franchises are so fun. … I could never do one now cause I’m just too old and brittle,” the 32-year-old told the crowd. Instead, she’s setting a new course. “I’m so happy that I eventually, finally, in my late 20s kind of just stopped and made some major changes, and I got the voice in my head back,” Lawrence reflected. “Now, it feels personal to me for the first time in a long time.” Jennifer Lawrence knows things got a bit weird there for a minute. April 24th, 2024   We are requesting a copy of San Francisco's Employee Compensation Report for the 2023   calendar year under the provisions of California Gov. Code § 7920, the California Public Records Act.    The purpose of this request is to obtain records which provide a complete and comprehensive account of San Francisco's total costs associated with employee full names and compensation.   Specifically, this request seeks an accounting, by full name and job title, of total gross wages paid to each employee and the total cost incurred separately by the employer for providing retirement and health benefits.    Note that the State Controller’s “Government Compensation in California” report does not contain the names of employees and therefore does not satisfy this request.    If your response is to send us a copy of that report, that will simply delay the process and take more of your time as we will reject it as insufficient to satisfy this request in full. As a reminder, per Gov. Code §7922.585(a) “Nothing in this section is intended to affect the public record status of information merely because it is stored in a computer. Public records stored in a computer shall be disclosed as required by this chapter.” Please provide the requested materials or, per Gov. Code   § 7922.535, a timeline along which they will be made available by, no later than ten days from the date of this request.    In an effort to standardize how this information  is reported, please include the following categories in your response:       Employee Name       (full name,       including first and last)      Position/Job       Title         (“City       Manager”, “Police Officer”, etc.)        Annual Salary       Minimum         & Maximum               Total Regular Pay        Overtime Pay     Other Pay (any       additional forms of pay       that are not reported in Regular Pay)      Retirement       Contribution         Costs - All       forms of employer-paid retirement contributions, deferred compensation,       etc., including Unaccrued Actuarial Liability if applicable.  Please       split out per the standard State Controller’s Office categories.             Healthcare       Contribution         Costs - All       forms of employer-paid health and welfare benefits, such as health, dental       and vision insurance benefits.    In the event San Francisco is not in possession of a record of this nature,  we request copies of any other record or records that contain information, even  if only in part, that is responsive to the purpose of this request — employee  name in conjunction with their compensation data for the period requested.   Per Gov. Code §7922.570(a), we ask that you provide the records in an Excel spreadsheet format. You may provide this data to us by replying to this email and attaching your data file.   There is no need to password-protect your responsive data, that data will be posted to a publicly-available website when we’ve completed our review process.   Note   that saving your original spreadsheet in the form of a PDF and sending that to us is not sufficient.   Doing this   will simply result in a need for you to take more time to respond, given that a PDF copy is not the original data, which is what we are requesting.  As   a reminder, Gov. Code §   7922.600(a)   instructs public agencies to "assist   requester in finding records and information that are responsive to the request or to the purpose of the request."   It   is not necessary to prepare a boilerplate PDF response document sent to us as an attachment to email in order to respond with your ETA. We are well aware of the legal provisions of the CPRA, do not need them reiterated, and are happy to accept a simple response   giving us the estimated date you will be able to provide the data requested.   Please   feel free to contact us with any questions that you might have.  Thank   you.  Municipalities   Researcher   Transparent   California  muni@transparentcalifornia.com     Rev   9/12/23

requests.request_text: Hello,  Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, I request the following records maintained by the Environmental Health Section's Housing/Habitability inspection program.   Complaint intake data, in the most granular electronic/exportable format available (e.g., CSV, Excel), for all mold, dampness, or moisture-related residential habitability complaints received by DPH from January 1, 2020, to present, including but not limited to the following fields where available:  Complaint/case number  Date complaint received  Property address (or, if full addresses are exempt, at minimum ZIP code and supervisorial district)  Complaint category/type (e.g., mold, water intrusion, dampness, ventilation)  Date of initial inspection  Date of any follow-up inspection(s)  Date case was closed/resolved  Outcome/disposition (e.g., violation found, no violation found, referred to code enforcement, voluntary correction)  Whether a private mold inspection/testing report was submitted as part of the case file, and if so, by which party (tenant or property owner/manager)  Property management company or owner of record, if captured in the case record    Any internal guidance, protocols, memoranda, or training materials used by DPH Environmental Health staff for evaluating privately-commissioned mold inspection reports (e.g., proprietary "mold index" or "mold score" type reports) submitted by property owners or tenants as part of a habitability complaint or inspection.  Any correspondence, complaints, or inquiries received by DPH from tenants, tenant advocacy organizations, or the public since January 1, 2022, expressing concern that a landlord-commissioned mold inspection report was used to dispute a tenant's habitability complaint or shift responsibility for mold conditions onto tenant behavior (e.g., ventilation habits, humidity, storage of personal property).  Any statistics or summary reports DPH has produced (internally or for the Board of Supervisors, Rent Board, or other bodies) analyzing citywide trends in mold/dampness complaints, including average time from complaint to resolution.   I request that records be provided electronically where feasible, in their native or a machine-readable format, to avoid duplication costs. If any of the requested categories exceed CPRA's statutory response timeframe due to volume, I am glad to discuss narrowing the date range or scope to expedite production, and would appreciate a phone or email conversation to that end.  Please contact me if any of the above requests require clarification, or if certain fields are only available via a formal data-sharing request outside standard CPRA production.  I appreciate your help!

However, for the Mayor's Office, the phrase "department head" refers to Mayor Breed, and ALSO, separately, each of Sean Elsbernd, Andrea Bruss, Hank Heckel, Andres Power, Andy Lynch, and Jeff Cretan. For the SFPD, "department head" refers to William Scott and ALSO, separately, each of Matt Dorsey and each assistant who sends or received email on behalf of Scott. Preserve, and do not permanently delete or allow to be deleted, at the time you receive this request, all records anywhere in your local deleted items, recycle bin, or similar folder on your local devices, and on your servers. Once you receive a request for records, it is illegal to allow them to be destroyed. Check your good government guide. A "device" includes all forms of computing - desktop, laptop, tablet, phone, server, etc., whether government or personal-owned. Each device and each app may have its own temporary space for deleted items. All must be searched.   You must provide a separate response to EACH request below for EACH person I have designated above. Combining the requests without specifying whether records exist for each person will result in a complaint for failure to provide a determination of the existence of requested records for each of my requests.   The request applies to government and personal accounts/devices - the latter to the extent that the records regard public business.  Let's see what the City likes deleting, or at least trying to delete.   REQUEST A: Under SFAC 67.21(c), produce within 7 days the required statement of form, existence, and quantity of:  (A.1) all emails or calendar items in your department head's recycle bin or deleted items folder or similar repository of attempted-to-be-deleted-but-not-permanently-deleted, whether on their local device OR on an IT server, with any timestamp  (A.2) all files in your department head's recycle bin or deleted items folder or similar repository of attempted-to-be-deleted-but-not-permanently-deleted, whether on their local device OR on an IT server, with any timestamp  (A.3) all emails in your department head's email account(s) with a subject line starting with "Not read:" with a timestamp from Jan 1, 2022 to present  (A.4) all texts or chats of any kind or app in your department head's recycle bin or deleted items folder or similar repository of attempted-to-be-deleted-but-not-permanently-deleted, whether on their local device OR on an IT server, with any timestamp   Each numbered item requires its own statement under 67.21(c). On the eighth day, a complaint will be filed. There are no extensions available under the law.   ====   For each of the email records below, you must produce (a) the record as an exact PDF copy preserving each email address and date/time stamp and attachments (in its own original electronic format as embedded in the email record), and also (b) with electronic metadata, namely the email headers. I am asking for rolling response - that means it is illegal for you to delay your response to (a) in order to produce the records in (b). For all non-email records, produce an exact copy in the original    REQUEST B: Produce for your department head:  (B.1) All records described in A.1 on a rolling basis from most recent to least recent.  (B.2) All records described in A.2 on a rolling basis from most recent to least recent.  (B.3) All records described in A.3 on a rolling basis from most recent to least recent.  (B.4) All records described in A.4 on a rolling basis from most recent to least recent.   If any of B.1 through B.4 would, on its own, produce more than 100 records for any one person, you may - while preserving all of the records - produce at first a listing of the subject lines or file names of all of the responsive records (screenshot, directory listing, however you would like) so I may downselect which I wish to receive a full copy of.   Do not refuse to respond because there are in your opinion too many records. Do not fail to start searching and producing records immediately because you may desire that I narrow the request later on. Complaints will be filed on the 11th day if no records have been started to be produced. Immediate Disclosure Request   SFGOV-0000011625 (IFB 23-2026)   On behalf of Capital Transit, I am submitting this Immediate Disclosure Request for records relating to Sourcing Event SFGOV-0000011625, Invitation for Bids (IFB) 23-2026, Non-Emergency Wheelchair-Accessible Transportation (NEWAT). I am counsel for Capital Transit.   This request is made under the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance (S.F. Admin. Code § 67.25) and the Department of Public Health's published public records policy ( https://www.sf.gov/get-public-records-dph). Under the Ordinance and the Department's policy, a response to an Immediate Disclosure Request is due by the close of the next business day.   On September 29, 2026, DPH issued Capital Transit a Notice of Non-Award for IFB 23-2026, stating that the City has issued a Notice of Intent to Award to Open Accessible Transport, 101 NEMT Inc, and Semax Enterprises as the three Lowest Responsive Bids. The contracting officers have told us to submit a request through NextRequest to obtain the winning proposals and bid tabulation so they can review the document request.   Under Section 11.10.3 of the IFB, a Notice of Protest of Contract Award must be submitted within three business days of the City's issuance of a Notice of Intent to Award, making Capital Transit's bid protest due on October 2, 2026. Section 11.10.3 also requires the protest to specify in detail each ground asserted and to include "facts and evidence sufficient for the City to determine the validity of the protest."  California courts treat bid protest procedures as a mandatory administrative remedy.  A bidder that does not follow those procedures on time may waive its right to challenge a contract award ( MCM Construction, Inc. v. City and County of San Francisco (1998) 66 Cal.App.4th 359 [78 Cal.Rptr.2d 44]).     Capital Transit cannot meaningfully evaluate or prepare a protest without the records described below.  Any delay beyond the Ordinance's timeline effectively denies Capital Transit its right to a fair protest process.    Please release the following records immediately, in electronic form:    The final bid tabulation and scoring rubric showing evaluated prices for all submitted bids.  The complete submitted Bids, including Bid Sheets and Minimum Qualifications documentation, of the three Bidders identified in the Notice of Intent to Award (Open Accessible Transport, 101 NEMT Inc, and Semax Enterprises).  All reviewer scorecards, price evaluation sheets, and determination records indicating how Capital Transit was ranked relative to the winning bidders.  All records reflecting the City's Minimum Qualifications determinations and any LBE Bid Discounts applied to each responsive Bid, including the documentation submitted under MQ #4 through MQ #9 by the three Bidders identified in the Notice of Intent to Award.    The California Constitution provides that the people have "the right of access to information concerning the conduct of the people's business."  It also requires that any authority limiting that right be narrowly construed (Cal. Const., art. I, § 3, subd. (b)). The California Public Records Act requires agencies to make public records "promptly available" (Gov.    Code, § 7922.530, subd.  (a)). It also provides that nothing in the Act permits an agency "to delay or obstruct the inspection or copying of public records" (Gov.  Code, § 7922.500). An agency that withholds any record bears the burden of justifying the withholding (Gov.  Code, § 7922.000).      The California Supreme Court has addressed when competitive proposals for public contracts must be disclosed.  It held that public disclosure may await the conclusion of the agency's negotiation process.  The Court also cited with approval the principle that proposals should be open for public inspection after contract award ( Michaelis, Montanari & Johnson v. Superior Court (2006) 38 Cal.4th 1065 [44 Cal.Rptr.3d 663, 136 P.3d 194]).  Here, IFB 23-2026 was an Invitation for Bids in which, according to DPH's notice, Minimum Qualifications were reviewed on a pass/fail basis and Bid Sheets were evaluated on lowest price after  LBE Bid Discounts. It was not a negotiated proposal process. (See Section 1.7 of the IFB provides that "City's Contract Terms are not subject to negotiation.")   According to DPH's own notice, the price evaluation is complete and the apparent low Bidders have been identified.  Withholding the Bids and bid tabulation now would serve no confidentiality interest in an ongoing competition, while it would prevent Capital Transit from evaluating whether a protest is necessary by the deadline.  Prompt disclosure also serves the core purposes of California's competitive bidding laws, which include eliminating favoritism, fraud, and corruption in the award of public contracts (Pub. Contract Code, § 100).   We recognize that Section 11.4 of the IFB states that Bids and related records "shall be open to inspection immediately after a contract has been awarded." That provision states when records must be made available at the latest; it does not prohibit earlier disclosure, and the same section confirms that all solicitation documents are subject to the Public Records Act and the Sunshine Ordinance. Any authority limiting the right of access must be narrowly construed (Cal. Const., art. I, § 3, subd. (b)(2)). Applying Section 11.4 to withhold records until after the protest period closes would make Section 11.10.3's requirement of "facts and evidence" impossible for any non-awarded Bidder to satisfy.    If DPH believes any portion of the requested records is exempt, please release all reasonably segregable, non-exempt portions immediately. Please also identify the specific legal authority for any redaction or withholding, as required by the Sunshine Ordinance and the Public Records Act.   We have also submitted to the email indicated on the SF.gov website at DPH.sunshine@sfdph.org.    Please provide the records by close of business tomorrow so that Capital Transit can exercise its right to protest if needed. If DPH cannot produce the records before the protest deadline, we request written confirmation that Capital Transit's protest period under Section 11.10.3 will be extended until the records are produced. If you have any questions, or if anything would prevent a timely response, please contact me right away.   Thank you for your prompt attention to this request.   Sincerely,   /Christopher Perez-Pruitt/  Christopher Perez-Pruitt

To the department heads of: City Attorney, DPW, DT, Mayor, Planning, Ethics Commission, DBI, Homelessness and Supportive Housing, DEM (including HSOC), HSA, DPH, City Administrator/GSA, SFPD, Sheriff, Rec&Park, District Attorney, Clerk of the Board, DPA, Controller, Treasurer-Tax Collector, Assessor-Recorder, OEWD, and PUC:   We're going to open up all the passive meetings to the entire public as required by law! For too long these have all been hidden.   1) This is an "inquiry" under Admin Code 67.4(a) (read the law carefully, it's not used often) for access to all meetings going forward of the following passive meeting bodies (the definitions below are from SFAC 67.3(d)) under the purview of your department, specifically:  (a) all "advisory committees created by the initiative of" your department head (which term also includes all past dept heads in such role in your dept),  (b) "any group that meets to discuss with or advise" your department head "on fiscal, economic, or policy issues" (very broad!), and  (c) all "committee[s] that consist[] solely of employees of the City and County of San Francisco when such committee is reviewing, developing, modifying, or creating City policies or procedures relating to the public health, safety, or welfare or relating to services for the homeless" that meets to discuss with or advise your department head or was created by the initiative of your department head.   I will be enforcing these clauses precisely as the words of the law say. If 2 or more persons (a "group"), including at least one person who is not a City employee, meet with a department head to discuss/advise on "fiscal, economic, or policy issues," that is a passive meeting body that you must give me access to attend - and yes that is very broad. Note that when you meet with public officials employed outside the City - such as SFUSD, SFBOE, City College, etc. - or any private persons, any group of those people ALSO qualifies.  But don't forget that some City employee-only groups ALSO qualify under (c). The only exception to allowing me access to observe all of these meetings is physical space (irrelevant virtually or on a phone) and where the meeting would otherwise meet a Brown Act closed session requirement (which includes very few topics and do NOT include all conferences with legal counsel, interestingly enough, but only those conferences with legal counsel regarding pending or anticipated litigation). To verify that you have fully provided me access to these meetings, I will later separately request your dept head's calendar - if any passive meetings exist on that calendar that you didn't give me access to, I will have proof that violated the law.   Each passive meeting you deny me access to after this inquiry may result in a complaint. I will file SOTF complaints if I don't hear back in a week. If access is not provided to passive meeting body gatherings as required by the Ordinance, Ethics Commission complaints will also be filed after 40 days. No further warning will be given.   NOTE: This item #1 is NOT a public records request. The usual public records deadlines don't apply to this inquiry, you can't just delay my access (which would prevent me from showing up) to meetings for 10, 24, etc. days. I've now "inquired" and that is all I am required to do for you to provide access to such meetings going forward. If you fail to provide me access to any such meeting (such as not providing conference call URL/pin/number, time, place) where it would be possible consistent with the facilities of such meeting for me to be present, I will file complaints. Every meeting with a virtual location or phone call number, at least, is physically accessible to me, and thus must be made available to me.   There are no extensions or rules of reason or any other excuses to prevent me from knowing about these meetings in a timely fashion. If you inform me about the meetings' URLs/phone numbers *after* they happen or refuse to provide me those by redacting them, I will allege that you unlawfully prevented me from attending after I inquired.  Unlike a public records request, you won't receive any more emails from me requesting each of these meeting entries, but will still have to allow me access to them going forward since I "inquired."   ============================   2) This is a SEPARATE immediate disclosure request for public information (for this, the records request deadlines apply), namely a list of all bodies meeting the definition in 1(a, b, or c) for your department.  You are required under the Sunshine Ordinance to provide both public records and also public information - defined as information contained in public records. It is possible that there is no separate existing record of such a list on its own. If there isn't, you can either simply inform me of which bodies meet the conditions above for your dept, or if you refuse, produce all public records that would reflect what I have asked, such as all invites for gatherings of each and every such body. Your choice. Since this is a public info request - you only have to produce info that exists already, not any new invites going forward that have not yet been created. The Missouri Department of Mental Health announced plans to relocate its Sex Offender Rehabilitation and Treatment Services (SORTS) program Tuesday to staff working in the unit. Debra Walker, director of public affairs for the agency, confirmed the plans in a statement to the News Tribune Tuesday afternoon.       The Missouri Legislature appropriated $15 million last year to renovate the hospital’s vacant Biggs Building. The renovated building would have housed the SORTS program.       Walker said moving the program was considered after it was determined renovating the Biggs Building for SORTS was “not the best use of state tax payers’ dollars.”       “Staffing challenges diminish the plans for that project,” she said.       Opened in 1851, Fulton State Hospital is the oldest public mental health facility west of the Mississippi River, according to its website. It houses a 300-bed treatment unit for high and intermediate security patients, units for individuals with developmental disabilities and the 125-bed SORTS unit.       The SORTS units provides treatment to people committed as sexually violent predators, according to the hospital’s 2021 services plan. Many have psychiatric and medical disorders and are treated with a full array of rehabilitation services.       The unit is contained within a secured perimeter of the Guhleman complex and patients can access the Cremer Activity Center for recreating activities, physical fitness, a library, a barber and beauty shop, vocational training and various medical clinics. Walker said the department made SORTS patients aware that it is considering different locations for the program.       No positions will be eliminated as a result of the move, Walker said, but the jobs of SORTS staff may change.       She said the move would take place “at some point in the future,” but timing and the new location have not been determined yet. The department is looking at options that can meet the space, workforce and treatment needs, she said.       “The DMH and FSH must consider realistic ways to meet these staffing and treatment demands,” Walker said.       There are more than 210 people sitting in county jails across the state waiting to be admitted to state-operated hospitals, Walker said.       For many, she added, Fulton State Hospital is the only place within the department’s system that can meet their individual needs.       “Staffing challenges have impacted DMH’s ability to admit individuals,” Walker said, “and FSH is experiencing some of the department’s biggest staffing shortages.”       DMH has been experiencing staffing shortages for years and officials largely attribute it to uncompetitive salaries.       State workers received a pay raise last year, which brought the minimum wage for all state workers to $15 per hour.       Gov. Mike Parson is suggesting another raise this year, which he said should help address the more than 7,000 open positions across state government.       The governor is proposing an 8.7 percent cost of living adjustment for all state employees and an increase in the shift differential – the extra bum in pay for employees working outside normal business hours – for congregate care staff within the Department of Social Service, Department of Corrections, Department of Mental health and the Missouri Veterans Commission.       “The $2 an hour shift differential for the congregate care workforce at 24/7 state operated programs is very important,” DMH Director Valerie Huhn said in a statement. “It acknowledges that increased pay is needed for the State of Missouri’s front line team members who work during hours when other staff are home with their families. The daily work these public servants do is vitally important to thousands of vulnerable citizens.” State relocating sex offender treatment program; planned renovation at Fulton State Hospital shelved. This is a follow-up request for additional documents pertaining to HSOC’s day-to-day operations to address homeless encampments and your agency’s particular role in that process. The time period for this request is July 1, 2018 to present. Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, Government Code § 6250, and the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance, San Francisco Administrative Code § 67.1, I hereby request as follows:     A.   All “bag and tag” logs identifying the property of homeless individuals removed and stored following HSOC or your agency’s resolution of any encampment or any street cleaning.     B.   All records identifying homeless property that is removed and stored by your agency, and information on how often that property is picked up or recovered by its owner.     C.   All memoranda, policies, schedules, or other documents identifying when and how your agency conducts street cleanings in the presence of a homeless encampment.     D.   All complaints, incident reports, incident tickets, or correspondence related to 311 or 911/0123 calls about homeless individuals or homeless encampments that have been referred to DPW for resolution or follow-up. Correspondence records should include both internal correspondence with other HSOC agencies, correspondence with “designated City forwarders,” and correspondence with complainants themselves. We do not seek any auto-populated, template responses or stock email responses. This request shall be limited to records from July 2021 to present.      E.    All correspondence related to homeless encampments sent between your agency and any of San Francisco’s seventeen (17) Community Benefit or Business Improvement Districts, or any of their present executive directors. Search terms should include, at a minimum, “encampment” or “tent.” For convenience, we provide a list of the current districts and their executive directors: Castro/Upper Market (Andrea Aiello), Civic Center (Tracy Everwine), Discover Polk (Duncan Ley/Ben Bleiman), Downtown (Robbie Silver), The East Cut (Andrew Robinson), Fisherman’s Whatf (Randall Scott), Japantown (Grace Horikiri), Lower Polk (Chris Schulman), Mid Market (Tracy Everwine), Moscone Expansion District (Paul Frentsos), Noe Valley (Debra Niemann), North of Market & Tenderloin (Simon Bertrang), Ocean Avenue (Pierre Smit), SoMa West (Christian Martin), Tourism Improvement District (Paul Frentsos), Union Square (Karin Flood), Yerba Buena (Cathy Maupin).     We expect an initial response to this records request on or before September 30, 2021. See Cal. Gov. Code § 6250; San Francisco Administrative Code § 67.21(b). After a preliminary discussion regarding your agency’s response, we welcome refining or adjusting our requests to better suit your agency’s existing data. See Cal. Gov. Code § 6253.1(a). Regardless, we expect that your agency will produce documents on a rolling basis as they become available. See San Francisco Administrative Code § 67.25(d). Please do not hesitate to reach out to us with any questions.

Hello,   My name is Daniel Giovenco and I am an Assistant Professor at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. I am interested in accessing historical data on tobacco retailer locations in San Francisco for an NIH-funded research project. This project will examine novel tobacco control policies in cities across the US and their impact on health equity. Commissioner Colfax provided a letter of support for our grant submission in 2022 (letter attached). Additionally, the City and County of San Francisco fulfilled our prior records request for the same dataset for the year 2023.     Below is a project summary that outlines our research objectives and other important information:   PROJECT SUMMARY   Background, rationale, and objectives: The local tobacco retail environment is a key driver of tobacco use behaviors and contributes to persistent health inequities. Several major cities across the US – including San Francisco – have recently implemented innovative policies to reduce the number of tobacco retailers in communities. Preliminary evidence from the San Francisco Tobacco-Free Project suggests that the City's policy is already making substantial progress in reducing residents' exposure to tobacco products and may serve as a model for other places considering similar policies. Our project seeks to compare rates of tobacco retailer density over time across several US cities with various tobacco retail reduction policies. Results can help identify “best practices” in policymaking and inform future tobacco control efforts. To that end, our specific objectives are to:     A)  Longitudinally measure changes in tobacco retailer density before and after policy implementation  B)   Examine the association between density reduction and neighborhood sociodemographic characteristics  C)   Compare rates of density reduction across cities with various types of tobacco retail reduction policies   Funding source: R01 grant from the National Cancer Institute at the National Institutes of Health     Description of data requested: Tobacco licensing data in the City of San Francisco for 2024 (i.e., list of retailers with active tobacco retail licenses in 2024). In order to properly geocode the retailers, we request store addresses and/or geographic coordinates. Other information, such as store name and store type, would also be useful, if available.     How data will be used: The retailer list would be geocoded using GIS software (e.g., QGIS) and merged with neighborhood-level data on sociodemographic characteristics (e.g., census data). The resulting dataset would be exported into a statistical software program (e.g., R, SAS) for analysis. We will remove any identifying store information (e.g., name, address) in our analyses.     How data will be stored: Data will be stored on password-protected, Columbia University-issued computers. These computers are fully encrypted and maintained by Columbia University’s IT department. We note that we have frequently worked with this type of data in the past, including tobacco licensing data from New York City, New Jersey, and Philadelphia. Only the study PI (Dr. Giovenco), primary data analyst, and project coordinator will have access to these datasets. No information that could identify stores (e.g., names, addresses) will be retained in the dataset after geocoding.     We are happy to provide more information about this project, if needed. Thank you for your support of health policy research!

Goodlett Place  City Hall, Room 200  San Francisco, CA 94102-4689   RE: Immediate Disclosure Request Related to Ballot Measure “Police Department Policies and Procedures” (Proposition E)   Dear Mayor Breed:   We write on behalf of the American Civil Liberties Union of Northern California with a public records request pursuant to the California Public Records Act, the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance, and Article I, § 3 of the California Constitution. We seek immediate disclosure of records related to the ballot measure titled “Police Department Policies and Procedures,” also known as Proposition E (“the Measure”).   Because this request concerns a pending ballot measure, it is crucial that you respond and provide records in a timely manner so that the public may understand the issues at stake. Accordingly, this letter constitutes an immediate disclosure request, and we look forward to your response by close of business on January 11, 2024.1   A. Requested Information   We seek the following records created on or after June 1, 2023 unless otherwise noted:   1. Text, email, and chat messages SENT or RECEIVED by Mayor Breed or the Mayor’s Chief of Staff regarding the Measure or the policies it contains;  2. Daily calendars2 of Mayor Breed and the Mayor’s Chief of Staff dated from July 1, 2023 to October 31, 2023 and including any notations, such as issues discussed or attendees;  3. Any communications, including correspondence or memorandums, RECEIVED by Mayor Breed or the Mayor’s Chief of Staff regarding the Measure or its policies from the U.S. Department of Justice or any other entity within the federal government;  4. Any communications, including correspondence or memorandums, RECEIVED by Mayor Breed or the Mayor’s Chief of Staff regarding the Measure or its policies from the California Department of Justice or any other entity within the state government; and  5. Any communications between Mayor Breed or any other representative of the Mayor’s Office with individuals or families impacted by police violence, police use of force, and/or SFPD surveillance practices and soliciting or receiving the input of those individuals or families for the Measure or the policies it contains.   In responding to this Request, please note that the CPRA broadly defines the term “record.” Specifically, the term includes “any writing containing information relating to the conduct of the people’s business prepared, owned, used, or retained by any state or local agency regardless of physical form or characteristics.”3 The CPRA defines, in turn, a “writing” as any “means of recording upon any tangible thing any form of communication or representation.”4 This Request therefore applies to all paper documents, as well as to all emails, videos, audio recordings, text messages, or other electronic records within the agency’s possession or control. Even if a record was created by a member of another government agency or a member of the public, it still must be produced so long as it is (or was) “used” or “retained” by the agency.5   As permitted by the CPRA, this Request sets forth the specific categories of information that we are seeking, rather than asking for documents by name.6 It is your obligation to conduct record searches based on the criteria identified herein.7 But should you come to believe that the present Request is overly broad, you are required to (1) offer assistance in identifying responsive records and information; (2) describe “the information technology and physical location in which the records exist;” and (3) provide “suggestions for overcoming any practical basis” that you assert as a reason to delay or deny access to the records or information sought.8   If you contend that an express provision of law exempts a responsive record from disclosure, either in whole or in part, you must make that determination in writing. Such a determination must specify the legal authority on which you rely, and must identify both the name and title of the person(s) responsible for the determination not to disclose.9    Additionally, even if you contend that a portion of a record requested is exempt from disclosure, you still must release the non-exempt portion of that record.10 Please note that the CPRA “endows” your agency with “discretionary authority to override” any of the Act’s statutory exemptions “when a dominating public interest favors disclosure.”11   Because the ACLU of Northern California is a non-profit organization and because this Request pertains to a matter of public concern, we request a fee waiver. None of the information obtained will be sold or distributed for profit. We also request that, to the extent possible, documents be provided in electronic format. Doing so will eliminate the need to copy the materials and provides another basis for the requested fee-waiver. If, however, you are unwilling to waive costs and anticipate that costs will exceed $50, or that the time needed to copy the records will delay their release, please contact us so that we can arrange to inspect the documents or decide which documents we wish to have copied and produced.   Otherwise, please copy and send all responsive records as soon as possible, and—if necessary—on a rolling basis, to egunn@aclunc.org or to Ellen Gunn, 39 Drumm St., San Francisco, CA 94111.   Thank you in advance for your assistance with this Request. If you require any clarification of this Request, please let us know. I have a number of questions relating to how “Facility Maintenance Funds” approved by the Capital Planning Committee are handled by the Controller’s Office, in addition to the requested records.      For this records request, please provide a): The current available balance in the Laguna Honda Hospital accounts for “Facilities Maintenance Funds” as of today’s date, June 11, or as of May 31, 2024; and b) The total amount of “Facility Maintenance Funds” awarded in each FY to LHH in each of the past five (5) fiscal years, starting in the current FY 2023–2024 and working backwards? The Missouri Department of Mental Health announced plans to relocate its Sex Offender Rehabilitation and Treatment Services (SORTS) program Tuesday to staff working in the unit. Debra Walker, director of public affairs for the agency, confirmed the plans in a statement to the News Tribune Tuesday afternoon.       The Missouri Legislature appropriated $15 million last year to renovate the hospital’s vacant Biggs Building. The renovated building would have housed the SORTS program.       Walker said moving the program was considered after it was determined renovating the Biggs Building for SORTS was “not the best use of state tax payers’ dollars.”       “Staffing challenges diminish the plans for that project,” she said.       Opened in 1851, Fulton State Hospital is the oldest public mental health facility west of the Mississippi River, according to its website. It houses a 300-bed treatment unit for high and intermediate security patients, units for individuals with developmental disabilities and the 125-bed SORTS unit.       The SORTS units provides treatment to people committed as sexually violent predators, according to the hospital’s 2021 services plan. Many have psychiatric and medical disorders and are treated with a full array of rehabilitation services.       The unit is contained within a secured perimeter of the Guhleman complex and patients can access the Cremer Activity Center for recreating activities, physical fitness, a library, a barber and beauty shop, vocational training and various medical clinics. Walker said the department made SORTS patients aware that it is considering different locations for the program.       No positions will be eliminated as a result of the move, Walker said, but the jobs of SORTS staff may change.       She said the move would take place “at some point in the future,” but timing and the new location have not been determined yet. The department is looking at options that can meet the space, workforce and treatment needs, she said.       “The DMH and FSH must consider realistic ways to meet these staffing and treatment demands,” Walker said.       There are more than 210 people sitting in county jails across the state waiting to be admitted to state-operated hospitals, Walker said.       For many, she added, Fulton State Hospital is the only place within the department’s system that can meet their individual needs.       “Staffing challenges have impacted DMH’s ability to admit individuals,” Walker said, “and FSH is experiencing some of the department’s biggest staffing shortages.”       DMH has been experiencing staffing shortages for years and officials largely attribute it to uncompetitive salaries.       State workers received a pay raise last year, which brought the minimum wage for all state workers to $15 per hour.       Gov. Mike Parson is suggesting another raise this year, which he said should help address the more than 7,000 open positions across state government.       The governor is proposing an 8.7 percent cost of living adjustment for all state employees and an increase in the shift differential – the extra bum in pay for employees working outside normal business hours – for congregate care staff within the Department of Social Service, Department of Corrections, Department of Mental health and the Missouri Veterans Commission.       “The $2 an hour shift differential for the congregate care workforce at 24/7 state operated programs is very important,” DMH Director Valerie Huhn said in a statement. “It acknowledges that increased pay is needed for the State of Missouri’s front line team members who work during hours when other staff are home with their families. The daily work these public servants do is vitally important to thousands of vulnerable citizens.” State relocating sex offender treatment program; planned renovation at Fulton State Hospital shelved. The story of Black History Month begins in 1915, half a century after the Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in the United States.      That September, the Harvard-trained historian Carter G. Woodson and the prominent minister Jesse E. Moorland founded the Association for the Student of Negro Life and History (ASNLH), an organization dedicated to researching and promoting achievements by Black Americans and other peoples of African descent.      Known today as the Association for the Study of African American Life and History (ASALH), the group sponsored a National History week in 1926, choosing the second week of February to coincide with the birthdays of Abraham Lincoln and Frederick Douglass. The event inspired schools and communities nationwide to organize local celebrations, establish history clubs and host performances and lectures.      In the decades that followed, mayors of cities across the country began issuing yearly proclamations recognizing “Negro History Week.” By the late 1960s, thanks in part to the civil rights movements and a growing awareness of Black identity, “Negro History Week” had evolved into Black History Month on many college campuses.  All policies, rules, regulations, manuals, handbooks, guidelines, and instructional materials related to homeless encampment removals and the seizure, storage, and/or destruction of personal property during homeless encampment removals. 
 
   
 
 All training materials given to and documents sufficient to show completion of training by employees involved in homeless encampment removals and the storage of personal property seized during encampment removals. 
 
   
 
 Documents sufficient to show which local ordinances, state statutes, or other laws were cited by the Department of Public Works or any other department as the basis for homeless encampment removals. 
 
   
 
 Documents reflecting data collected before, during, or after a sweep including but not limited to number and demographic information of homeless people moved out of encampments. 
 
   
 
 All communications (i.e. meeting minutes, e-mails, mail, etc.) made within the Department of Public Works and between the Department and other departments using the terms “encampment resolution,” “encampment removal,” and/ or “bag and tag” from July 1, 2017, to the present. 
 
   
 
 Any notices, informational materials, or referral forms given to homeless people before, during, or after a homeless encampment removal.

Hi, I live at 101 Graystone Terr San Francisco 94114 and my home has 2 apartments one of which has its entrance off the Pemberton Place Steps at 45 Pemberton. Along the two short flights of cement steps going from Graystone down towards Villa (actually it may effect all the steps) is a broken down, man-made watering, irrigation system that has been defunct for quite a while decades I think, until recently. The tenant at 45 Pemberton says that suddenly on Wednesday mornings the system comes alive and  due to its neglected condition the water collects in a pool near her entrance and spills down the cement steps for a couple of hours…  problem #2 where that same pool of water collects  before  the entrance to 45 Pemberton is a drain and the pipes it’s connected to (city pipes) seem to take the water from all of my properties sinks and toilets and carries it down the hill to wherever it goes. Every year there are times that drain backs up and spills sewage water out onto the landing and down the entire length of the steps to Villa. This has happened twice in the last month. I contact 311 and within an hour they unclog the drain (or as much as they can reach) and power wash the steps  which helps but never completely cleans away the human waste. I’m wanting to find some history of this part of the San Francisco water and sewage system. When it was installed, which properties are served by which pipes and also any history pertaining to what I’ve been told is a natural underground spring (??) that runs from above Graystone down along the Pemberton steps (or close to it) and that empties onto the bottom of the steps at Clayton between Corbett and Twin Peaks Blvd closer to Corbett and across the street from a small community garden.   Part of me is simply curious about the history( my family’s lived at 101 Graystone Terr since 1958 and most of me wants to understand the old water system in order to request an upgrade! Of course. I want to emphasize that recently ,since the Pandemic, the Pemberton Steps have become a real destination for local and visiting walkers, runners and San Francisco enthusiasts. Now I see to 3 or 4 dozen walkers  per day. The steps have come  into their own, as it were and we neighbors love it. We love sharing our secret with others daring to make the climb, we love the attention and diversity that comes along. I’ve seen 3 couples taking their wedding photos on the Pemberton Steps as well as class field trips, skater kids, seniors, dog walkers abound, happy couples, unhappy couples that find happy, deep thinkers, stunned locals muttering “I’ve lived here my whole life and never even heard of these steps!” Or “only in San Francisco will you see such a marvel!” People respect the steps and care about them and it’s a shame when they have to step carefully or even turn around because of the sewage oozing down…that’s why I’m interested. I want to begin the process before the steps become an eyesore, a health hazard or one of those San Francisco treats that is no longer…  I hope this is a good place to start.  Respectfully,  Jason Kordelos   101 Graystone Terr   San Francisco ca 94114   415-261-2991
