Xenophobia itself came to us by way of New Latin and first appeared in print in English in the late 19th century. Merriam-Webster Dictionary.: https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/xenophobia               [v]                      Common Myths About Diversity and Cultural Competency        Myth # 1: There are too many cultures in the US and world. I cannot possibly learn what I need to know about all of them.   Cultural competence does not mean learning as many “characteristics” as possible about every culture. In fact, to the contrary, the process of cultural competence means that a person (1) learns to recognize and reject his or her preexisting beliefs about a culture, (2) learns to recognize the influence of their own culture on creating those beliefs about other cultures, (3) focuses on understanding information provided by individuals within the context at hand (e.g., patient, front desk, etc.) and (4) forgoes the temptation to classify or label persons with cultural names. This process makes cultural competence a more manageable task that avoids fixed, generalized cultural misinformation.      Myth # 2: I have examined my preconceptions about the various cultures in my service area, changed some of my thoughts, and now feel culturally competent to deal with people who might appear in my clinic and/or organization.   Cultural competence is not a one-time, finite achievement. It is a life long process that is reapplied in every interaction. The process must be practiced throughout one’s career, it must be re-examined periodically by organizations. It would be dangerous for a person or organization to conclude that he/she or they have learned all there is to know about certain cultures, has reached the point of cultural competence, or has even identified (i.e., labeled) all the potentially different cultures in the local/national community. Regardless of the amount learned about a different culture, the individual person’s experience within that culture is unique.      Myth # 3: My own diversity, be it my ethnicity, my gender or my disability has taught me what it means to be culturally sensitive. I don’t need any special training on how to become cultural competent.   Each person has different levels of awareness and sensitivity about his or her own diversity or culture. Every human being, however, holds preconceptions about “different” cultures or dimensions of diversity. Every person, including a person outside the dominant culture, must use some kind of deliberate, analytical process to examine cultural misinformation and strive for cultural competence in each individual case.      Myth #4: We are already a diverse organization, so there is nothing left to be done.   Organizations are a microcosm of society, and if that is the case, then we can hardly buy into the idea that the shared and unique cultural and personal differences among employees in any particular corporate or non-profit organization are somehow readily accepted and seldom an issue or source of conflict. In fact, as organizations have become more diverse, the number of conflicts based on difference may have very well increased due to the lack of understanding and awareness about the vast dimensions of diversity people bring to work and their interplay in the workplace. Being a diverse organization is an important first step, but just as important is learning how to include and leverage that diversity to the benefit of the organization.      Myth # 5: I need a more concrete way to achieve cultural competence. This process is too “touchy feely” in asking me to become more aware. How do I become aware? How will that make a difference in my journey towards cultural competence?  Awareness means knowledge of the existence of a thing, place, idea, etc. Awareness begins with the willingness to learn. The professional’s first step toward cultural competence in handling a situation is to become aware that he or she might have stereotypes or preconceptions about the person before him or her. Awareness is a complex skill gained over time. Only with greater cultural awareness can a person reject or avoid acting on the preconceived thoughts, obtain new individualized information and resolve the case with cultural competence.      Myth # 6: There are only a couple of cultures that are different from the dominant (American) culture in my community.  Culture is not defined exclusively by race and ethnicity. It includes a broad spectrum of identities. Regardless of the perceived diversity or lack of diversity in one’s community, every person encounters people in on a daily basis with cultural experiences that differ from their own. Using a process to practice cultural competence routinely in every case can help a person ensure fair and equal treatment of every person who comes before them for assistance.      Myth #7: Diversity equals preferential treatment for others, and doesn’t do anything to benefit me or others in the majority.          Diversity is the collective mixture of differences and similarities among all individuals in an organization. Diversity pertains to each and every one of us, and therefore, an effective program should be inclusive-enabling everyone to have an equal voice and an equal opportunity to utilize their talents. Organizations that are making great strides in creating work environments that support diversity, and are implementing innovative people practices that provide opportunities for everyone, including women and minority staff are also the very same organizations that are winning praise and recognition for innovative, employee-focused programs that are highly valued and beneficial to all.      Myth # 8: I already attended all those legal “don’t do” trainings such as discrimination training, sexual harassment training, and disability rights training. So I know what the law says you can and cannot do.  Cultural Competency is not about behaviors governed by law, it is about behaviors and actions that improve a person’s ability to effectively and authentically communicate and interact with people perceived to be different. Cultural competency is about what you “can do” to improve the services and outcomes of people who come to you for assistance. A rule pertaining to Cultural Competency that one should strive to follow is the “Platinum Rule” which states, “do unto to others as they would want to be done unto.” Learn what others want by becoming aware, asking questions, and seeking out information in an authentic and respectful way.      Common Myths About Diversity and Cultural Competency. National Council on Disability (NCD).: https://www.ncd.gov/fact%20sheets/2006/06/01/common-myths-about-diversity-and-cultural-competency/              [vi] It is well known, of course, that race and insanity share a long and troubled past. In the 1850s, American psychiatrists believed that African American slaves who ran away from their white masters did so because of a mental illness called drapetomania. Medical journals of the era also described a condition called dyaestheia eathiopis, a form of madness manifest by “rascality” and “disrespect for the master’s property” that was believed to be “cured” by extensive whipping. Even at the turn of the twentieth century, leading academic psychiatrists shamefully claimed that “Negroes” were “psychologically unfit for freedom.” (…)      As a beginning illustration of the book’s main point, consider a prominent story that appeared on the front page of the Washington Post on June 28th 2005. “Racial Disparities Found in Pinpointing Mental Illness” read the headline. The article detailed a discovery that was at once shocking and sadly familiar. Researchers had examined the largest American registry of psychiatric patient records looking for “ethnic trends” in schizophrenia diagnoses. As the Post described it, schizophrenia, “a disorder that often portends years of powerful brain altering drugs, social ostracism and forced hospitalizations…has been shown to affect all ethnic groups at the same rate.” And yet, the large government study uncovered striking categorical differences in its analysis of 134,523 case files: doctors diagnoses schizophrenia in African American patients, and particularly African American men, four times as often as in white patients. The Post cited the study’s lead author, John Zeber, who explained that doctors overdiagnoses schizophrenia in African American men even though the research team uncovered no evidence that “black patients were sicker than whites,” or that patients in either group were more likely suffer from drug addiction, poverty, depression, or a host of other variables. According to Zeber, “the only factor that was truly important was race.”       Paradoxically, we live in an era when the opposite is supposed to be the case: race should be entirely unimportant to psychiatric diagnosis. (…) Meanwhile, textbooks routinely claim that, as a biological disorder, schizophrenia is an illness that should occur in 1 percent of any given population, or one out of every hundred persons regardless of where they live, how they dress, who they know, or what type of music they happen to prefer. Yet, in the real world, 1 percent is a delusion. Not only do stories such as the Post article appear with regularity – they persist over time. In the 1960s, National Institute of Mental Health studies found that “blacks have a 65% higher rate of schizophrenia than whites.” In 1973, a series of studies in the Archives of General Psychiatry discovered that African Americans patients were “significantly more likely” than white patients to receive diagnoses for other mental illnesses such as depression or bipolar disorder. Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, a host of articles from leading psychiatric and medical journals showed that doctors diagnosed the paranoid subtype of schizophrenia in African American men five to seven times more often than in white men, and also more frequently than in other ethnic minority groups.       Everyday racism seems a reasonable explanation for these findings. Though we might wish otherwise, medical training does not wholly free clinicians from preexisting racial beliefs, assumptions, or blind spots. While medicine has undoubtedly made significant progress toward addressing multicultural issues in clinical practice, some doctors undoubtedly harbor negative opinions about particular patients based on stereotyped cultural assumptions. As Francis Lu, a psychiatrist at the University of California at San Francisco, explains it “physician bias is a very real issue… we don’t talk about it – it’s upsetting. We see ourselves as unbiased and rational and scientific.”       This book makes a broader claim: from a historical perspective, race impacts medical communication because racial tensions are structured into clinical interactions long before doctors or patients enter examination rooms. To a remarkable extent, anxieties about racial difference shape diagnostic criteria, health-care policies, medical and popular attitudes about mentally ill persons, the structures of treatment facilities, and, ultimately, the conversations that take place there within. (…) In a perfect world, interactions between doctors and patients should be immune from any process deemed destructive to health. The Hippocratic Oath decrees that the primary aim of medical encounters is to restore, not to harm. Most physicians (….) enter the practice of medicine out of a desire to help people. And most patients seek the aid of physicians in times when they require palliation and care. However, as the pages that follow reveal, institutional forces supersede even the best individual intentions when race and insanity are the topics of diagnostic interaction. (…)       Prior to the civil rights movement, mainstream American medical and popular opinion often assumed that patients with schizophrenia were largely white, and generally harmless to society. From the 1920s to the 1950s, psychiatric textbooks depicted schizophrenia as an exceedingly broad, general condition, manifest by “emotional disharmony,” that negatively impacted white people’s abilities to “think and feel.” Authors of research articles in leading psychiatric journals, many of whom were psychoanalysts, described patients with schizophrenia, and, all too often, their “schizophrenogenic mothers,” as “native-born Americans” or immigrants of “white European ancestry.” Psychiatric authors frequently assumed that such patients were nonthreatening, and were therefore to be psychoterapeutically nurtured by their doctors, as if unruly children, but certainly not feared.       Leading mainstream American newspapers in the 1920s to the 1950s similarly described schizophrenia as an illness that occurred “in the seclusive, sensitive person with few friends who has been the model of behavior in childhood,” or that afflicted white women or intellectuals. In 1935, for instance, the New York Times described how many white poets and novelists demonstrated a symptom called “grandiloquence,” a propensity toward flowery prose believed to be “one of the telltale phrases of schizophrenia, the mild form of insanity known as split personality.” Meanwhile, popular magazines such as Ladies’ Home Journal and Better Homes and Gardens wrote of unhappily married, middle class white women whose schizophrenic mood swings were suggestive of “Doctor Jekyll and Mrs. Hyde,” a theme that also appeared in Olivia de Havillans’s infamous depiction of a “schizophrenic housewife” named Virginia Stuart Cunningham in the 1948 Anatole Litvak film, the Snake Pit.       Of course, it was far from the case that all persons who suffered from a disease called schizophrenia during the first half of the twentieth century were members of a category called white. Rather, American culture marked schizophrenia as a disease of the mainstream in ways that encouraged identification with certain groups of people while rendering other groups invisible. For example, popular magazines in the 1920s to the 1950s incorrectly assumed that schizophrenia was a psychoanalytic condition connected to neurosis, and as a result affixed the term to middle-class housewives. Meanwhile, researchers conducted most published clinical studies in white-only wards. Such strategies occluded recognition of the countless men and women diagnosed with schizophrenia who resided in so-called Negro hospitals and suffered well outside most realms of public awareness.       American assumptions about the race, gender, and temperament of schizophrenia changed beginning in the 1960s. Many leading medical and popular sources suddenly described schizophrenia as an illness manifested not by docility, but by rage. Growing numbers of research articles from leading psychiatric journals asserted that schizophrenia was a condition that also afflicted “Negro men,” and that black forms of the illness were marked by volatility and aggression. In the worse cases, psychiatric authors conflated the schizophrenic symptoms of African American patients with the perceived schizophrenia of civil rights protests, particularly those organized by Black Power, Black Panthers, Nation of Islam, or other activist groups.       As but one example, the title of this book comes from a 1968 article that appeared in the prestigious Archives of General Psychiatry, in which psychiatrists Walter Bromberg and Frank Simon described schizophrenia as a “protest psychosis” whereby Black men developed “hostile and aggressive feelings” and “delusional anti-whiteness” after listening to the words of Malcolm X, joining the Black Muslims, or aligning with groups that preached militant resistance to white society. According to the authors, the men required psychiatric treatment because their symptoms threatened not only their own sanity, but the social order of white America. requests.request_text: I am Erika Carlos, a reporter for El Tecolote. I ask that you acknowledge receipt of this records request once it is received, and ask for a determination before or on August 14, 2025, per the Sunshine Ordinance, and an even faster reply if you can make that determination without having to review the record(s) in question.   Pursuant to the California Public Records Act (“CPRA”)[Gov’t Code §§ 7920.530 et seq.], the California Constitution,[Cal. Const., art. I, § 3(b)(1)], and the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance (SEC. 67.20 et seq.) I, therefore, request the following records in the “possession, control of, relating to, to be about, or to bear on” the City of San Francisco from July 28 to August 4, 2025.   1)All records of communications 'sent by’ city employees Abel Simon, Patrick Fosdahl, Nhi Tu and Jennifer Callewaert about vending in the city, from their work and personal devices, during the specified time.   As used in this Request, “communications” includes: a) Memos, b) Reports, c) Notes, d)Email messages (including attachments, calendar invites, and attachments to calendar invites), and e) Text messages (including attachments).   f) For each responsive record, please provide the entire email thread or conversation chain it belongs to, including all preceding and subsequent replies, forwards, and responses from city staff and officials. This is to ensure full context for each communication.   DELIVERY: Please provide records in their original format and in a folder for each city employee. For example, emails on a .msg file with their attachments, photos, text documents on a word-searchable PDF file –– capable of Online Text Recognition, and quantitative data in a manipulatable, searchable Excel (XLS) spreadsheet.”   Also please note, the City of San Jose v. Superior Court (2017) case in which the California Supreme Court unanimously held the public has a right to see emails and text messages pertaining to public affairs that are sent from, or received on, government employees and officials personal devices and email accounts. A public record is still a public record no matter where it is kept, how it was transmitted or where it is retained.   As permitted by the CPR, this request sets forth the specific categories of information that we are seeking, rather than asking for documents by name [Gov’t Code § 6253(b)]. It is your obligation to conduct record searches based on the criteria identified herein [See id. §§ 6253–6253.1]. But should you come to believe that the present request is overly broad, you are required to (1) offer assistance in identifying responsive records and information; (2) describe “the information technology and physical location in which the records exist;” and (3) provide “suggestions for overcoming any practical basis” that you assert as a reason to delay or deny access to the records or information sought [Id. § 6253.1(a)].   The CPRA requires that you respond to this request in ten days. [Id. § 6253(c)] "No notice shall specify a date that would result in an extension for more than 14 days." [Cal. Gov. Code § 7922.535(b)-(c)]   If you contend that an express provision of the law exempts a responsive record from disclosure, either in whole or in part, you must make that determination in writing. Such a determination must specify the legal authority on which you rely, as well as identify both the name and title of the person(s) responsible for the determination not to disclose.[Id. § 6255; see also id. § 6253(d)(3)]    Additionally, even if you contend that a portion of a record requested is exempt from disclosure, you still must release the non-exempt portion of that record. [Id. § 6253(a), (c)]   Please note that the CPRA “endows” your agency with “discretionary authority to override” any of the Act’s statutory exemptions “when a dominating public interest favors disclosure.” [ CBS, Inc. v. Block, 42 Cal. 3d 646, 652 (1986); see also Nat’l Conference of Black Mayors v. Chico Cmty. Publ’g, Inc., 25 Cal. App. 5th 570, 579 (2018) (construing the CPRA’s exemptions as “permissive, not mandatory—they allow nondisclosure but do not prohibit disclosure”)]   Because this request pertains to a matter of public concern, I request a fee waiver. None of the information obtained will be sold or distributed for profit. I also request that, to the extent possible, documents be provided in electronic format. Doing so will eliminate the need to copy the materials and provide another basis for the requested fee waiver.    Please copy and send all responsive records as soon as possible, and—if necessary—on a rolling basis to this public records portal. If you have any questions, please email me.  Thank you in advance for your assistance with this request, and I look forward to hearing from you in ten days: August 14, 2025.

March 8, 2024   Dr. Hillary Kunins  Director, Behavioral Health Services and Mental Health SF  San Francisco Department of Public Health   1380 Howard St.   San Francisco, CA 94103   Re: Public Records Act Request    Dear Dr. Kunins:   Pursuant to California Public Records Act, Government Code Sections 6250 et seq., Disability Rights California (DRC) requests copies of public records identified herein, including but not limited to any written materials, photographs, electronic data, and communications, in the possession or control of the San Francisco Department of Public Health related to implementation of SB 43 (2023).   This request does not seek confidential information. If you determine that any other information qualifies for an exemption from disclosure, please note the basis for the claimed exemption, redact the material at issue for the time being, and make the rest available as requested. Please also provide a signed notification citing the legal authorities on which you rely if you determine that any responsive information is exempt and will not be disclosed.    DEFINITIONS   SB 43 means California Senate Bill (SB) 43 signed by the Governor on October 10, 2023. SB 43 expanded the definition of Grave Disability in Welfare & Institutions Code § 5008(h). Mayor London Breed issued an executive order directing San Francisco City and County departments, including the Department of Public Health, to prepare for SB 43 implementation on January 1, 2024.[1]    DOCUMENTS means and includes both paper documents and electronic representations of information, including handwriting, typewriting, printing, photographing, photocopying, transmitting by electronic mail, text messaging, instant messaging, or facsimile, and every other means of recording upon any tangible thing, any form of communication or representation, including letters, words, pictures, videos, sounds, recordings, or symbols, or combinations thereof, and any records thereby created, regardless of which method the record has been stored.     POLICIES AND PROCEDURES means policies, procedures, criteria, or practices, whether written or established through custom or use, including but not limited to policy and procedure manuals, protocols, directives, flowcharts, institution post orders, training materials, and any other public records designed to direct the actions of the San Francisco employees, personnel, and contractors.   SCOPE OF REQUEST   Unless otherwise specified, we seek copies of records the Department of Public Health’s possession, regardless of who wrote them, from September 1, 2023 to the present.   If multiple versions of the same DOCUMENT exist, we seek copies of every version of each that has existed from September 1, 2023 to the present.   RECORDS REQUEST    The public records we request are as follows:    1.   All DOCUMENTS, including drafts, related to implementation of SB 43 in San Francisco City and County, including POLICIES AND PROCEDURES, communications, reports, data, trainings, and directives.    Please send a response within 10 days, as required by Government Code section 6253(c), to my attention at the address indicated below. For any and all responsive records that are available in electronic format, please produce electronic copies of the records.   Please send all electronic records to Samuel.Jain@disabilityrightsca.org.     Disability Rights California is a nonprofit organization mandated by federal and state law to assist persons with disabilities. The requested information is not sought for commercial purposes and its disclosure serves the public interest in ensuring the health, safety, and welfare of people with disabilities. We therefore kindly request a waiver of any copying charges. If any costs will be imposed, please notify me in advance, so that we may decide how to proceed.   If you have any questions or concerns regarding this request, please contact me:                      Disability Rights California                      ATTN: Samuel Jain                      1831 K Street                      Sacramento, CA 95811                      Telephone: (916) 549-5929                     Samuel.Jain@disabilityrightsca.org    Thank you in advance for your consideration and prompt attention to this request.    Sincerely,   Samuel Jain  Senior Attorney  Disability Rights California      [1] https://www.sf.gov/sites/default/files/2023-12/San%20Francisco%E2%80%99s%20Implementation%20of%20New%20Conservatorship%20Law%20%282%29.pdf.

ALPR Audit, Access, and Data-Sharing Records   To: Public Records Custodian  Agency: San Francisco Police Department   Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, Government Code § 7920.000 et seq., I request copies of the following existing records concerning the San Francisco Police Department's use of automated license plate recognition ("ALPR") technology.   For purposes of this request, "ALPR" includes systems, services, or platforms supplied or operated by vendors including, but not limited to, Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions / Vigilant Solutions, Digital Recognition Network (DRN), Leonardo / ELSAG, Rekor, Vaxtor, Genetec, or any other ALPR vendor used by the Department.   The requested period for audit and activity records is January 1, 2026 through August 31, 2026.   1. ALPR Search / Organization Audit Records   Please provide existing audit logs, search logs, access logs, usage reports, or equivalent records documenting ALPR searches performed by users of the San Francisco Police Department's ALPR system during the requested period.   This includes, where maintained:    organization-level audit exports;  user search-history exports;  query audit logs;  access logs;  administrative audit records; and  equivalent vendor-specific audit reports.    For Flock Safety systems, this includes the Organization Audit export or equivalent.   Please provide the existing native electronic export, preferably CSV, XLSX, JSON, or another structured machine-readable format rather than a PDF conversion.   2. External / Network Access Audit Records   Please provide existing records documenting searches of or access to the San Francisco Police Department's ALPR data by users, agencies, organizations, or networks outside the Department during the requested period.   This includes:    network audit logs;  external-agency query logs;  federated-search audit records;  interagency access logs; and  equivalent vendor-specific exports.    For Flock Safety systems, this includes the Network Audit export or equivalent.   3. Current ALPR Data-Sharing Configuration   Please provide existing records reflecting the Department's current ALPR data-sharing, network-access, or federated-search configuration, including records identifying:    agencies or organizations with which the Department shares ALPR access;  agencies or organizations sharing ALPR access with the Department;  regional, statewide, or nationwide ALPR networks in which the Department participates;  fusion centers or real-time crime centers with access;  federal, state, county, municipal, tribal, or task-force access; and  configured sharing groups, partner organizations, or network permissions.    For Flock Safety systems, this includes, where maintained:    SharedNetworks.csv;  "Networks Shared With Me";  "Networks I'm Sharing"; and  equivalent sharing or organization-access exports.    4. Administrative / Configuration Audit Records   Please provide existing administrative, configuration, or event audit records during the requested period reflecting additions, removals, or modifications involving:    network-sharing relationships;  authorized agencies or organizations;  user or administrator access;  statewide or nationwide access;  retention settings;  federated-search permissions;  hotlists or watchlists; or  integrations affecting ALPR access or sharing.    For Flock Safety systems, this includes the Event Log or equivalent administrative audit export.   5. Vendor, Product, and Retention Identification   Please provide any existing record sufficient to identify:    the ALPR vendor or vendors currently used;  the ALPR product, platform, service, or module currently used;  any regional/interagency ALPR network in which the Department participates; and  the currently configured ALPR data-retention period.    A current order form, product list, administrative configuration record, contract page, invoice, or similar existing record is sufficient.   Electronic Format / Redaction   Where responsive records exist as CSV, XLSX, JSON, XML, or another structured electronic export, I request the records in that existing electronic format rather than converted to PDF.   This request seeks existing records and does not ask the Department to create new statistics, conduct new analysis, or construct a new database.   I am not requesting bulk ALPR detection imagery or a database of motorists' historical locations.   If a particular field—such as a license plate/query value, personal identifier, or other protected information—is exempt, please redact only that information and provide the remaining nonexempt portions, including where applicable timestamps, organization information, search purposes, search scope, sharing relationships, event types, and remaining row/column structure.   If any responsive records are withheld in whole or part, please identify the statutory authority supporting the withholding or redaction.   If anticipated fees exceed $25, please provide an estimate before incurring the cost.   Electronic rolling production is welcome.   Thank you,   Sergio Medeiros  sergio.medeiros@owasp.org

In light of the San Francisco Health Commission meeting held on Monday, February 2nd, and the unresolved lack of clarity regarding statements made during that meeting, I am writing to formally request written clarification concerning the San Francisco Department of Public Health’s proposed reductions to BHSA-aligned workforce development and workforce equity programs.     Specifically, I am requesting clarification on the following:  •	BHSA Workforce Development & Statutory Compliance  BH-Connect Workforce, Fidelity & Reimbursement Risk  Implementation vs. Instruction  Equity, Disparate Impact & Accountability  Governance, Process & Oversight   1.	What BHSA-compliant alternatives were evaluated before recommending reductions to Workforce Education and Training (WET)–funded workforce development and workforce equity contracts? Please identify and describe all funding-related scenarios developed and evaluated between October 2025 and the present as alternatives to reducing or eliminating workforce development and workforce equity contracts, including any scenarios designed to preserve compliance with BHSA Workforce Education and Training (WET) statutory requirements. If no such alternatives were evaluated, please state that explicitly.   2.	What legal or statutory analysis supports treating workforce development as discretionary or optional under the Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA / Proposition 1)?   3.	How does dismantling workforce development and workforce equity infrastructure align with San Francisco’s approved BHSA plans and workforce development commitments submitted to the State?   4.	How does the San Francisco Department of Public Health plan to meet BHSA workforce requirements without funding implementation functions such as supervision, stipends, coordination, training logistics, and workforce stabilization supports?   5.	Has the Department received written guidance from the State indicating that BHSA workforce development funds may be reduced or reallocated away from workforce development purposes? If so, when was this guidance received? When will that guidance be shared publicly?   6.	How does the Department plan to meet BH-Connect workforce development and fidelity requirements, particularly for ACT, FACT, and FSP-aligned services, without dedicated workforce development infrastructure and implementation funding?   7.	What assessment has been conducted regarding the risk that reducing workforce development investments could impair San Francisco’s ability to meet BH-Connect model fidelity thresholds required for bundled Medi-Cal reimbursement?   8.	How does the San Francisco Department of Public Health reconcile proposed workforce development cuts with BH-Connect’s reliance on multidisciplinary, team-based staffing models that assume a trained, stable, and adequately supported workforce?   9.	What contingency plans exist if reductions in workforce development funding result in delays to BH-Connect implementation timelines or loss of bundled reimbursement eligibility?   10.	How does the Department assess workforce development under BH-Connect—as a compliance requirement, a financial sustainability strategy, or both—and how is that assessment reflected in current budget recommendations?   11.	How does the Department distinguish between state-provided instructional training and the local implementation costs required to operationalize that training, including staff time, supervision, accreditation, coordination, and technology?   12.	What funding source is proposed to cover these implementation and operational costs if WET-funded workforce development programs are eliminated or reduced?   13.	Has the Department evaluated whether eliminating local workforce development funding creates an unfunded mandate that undermines the effectiveness of state-provided training?   14.	What equity impact analysis has been conducted to assess whether proposed workforce development reductions disproportionately affect peer workforce roles, equity-centered programs, or services supporting Black San Franciscans?   15.	How does the Department reconcile proposed workforce development cuts with publicly acknowledged data showing significantly higher rates of Black infant mortality and Black overdose deaths in San Francisco?   16.	What accountability mechanisms exist if local workforce funding decisions exacerbate disparities in health outcomes for Black San Franciscans or other disproportionately impacted communities?   17.	What role does the San Francisco Health Commission have in reviewing and approving reductions to state-mandated workforce funding, and what documentation will be provided to support that oversight responsibility?   18.	Why were impacted contractors and workforce partners not uniformly notified or briefed prior to meetings discussing potential workforce funding reductions?   19.	How does the Department ensure transparency and due process when proposed cuts affect contracts previously approved for extension by the Civil Service Commission?   These questions are raised in direct connection to the findings and recommendations outlined in the Undoing Racism: A Tactical Guide to Advancing Fair Employment, Civil Rights Compliance, and Health Equity report previously submitted to the Department (also attached). That report documents longstanding disparities in workforce treatment, leadership accountability, and health outcomes for Black San Franciscans, and explicitly identifies workforce equity and leadership accountability infrastructure as necessary conditions for ethical, compliant, and effective service delivery. Decisions to dismantle workforce development and equity functions without addressing these documented risks raise serious concerns regarding compliance, equity, and public accountability.     Given the significance of these decisions and their potential impact on workforce stability, service access, and health equity, a written response is respectfully requested. Senators Buckley and Pell sponsored major FERPA amendments that were enacted on December 31st 1974, just four months later, and made retroactive to its effect date of November 19th 1974. These amendments were intended to address a number of ambiguities and concerns identified by the educational community, including parents, students and institutions. (…)     In 1990, Congress enacted the Campus Security Act, which added a new exception to the prior written consent rule: post-secondary institutions may disclose to an alleged victim of any crime of violence (as defined in U.S Code Title 18, Section 16) the results of any disciplinary proceeding conducted by the institution against the alleged perpetrator of the crime, regardless of the outcome of the proceeding. Congress amended this provision in the Higher Education Amendments of 1998 by including “nonforcible sex offenses” and clarifying that only “final results” may be disclosed (i.e., name of student perpetrator, violation committed, and sanction imposed. Written consent is still required to disclose the name of any other student).      The following new exception was also added in the 1998 HEA amendments: post-secondary institutions may disclose the final results of any disciplinary proceeding for a crime of violence (as defined above) or nonforcible sex offense to anyone, including members of the general public, if the institution determines that the student committed a violation of its rules or policies with respect to the crime.      The 1998 HEA amendments also added a new exception that allows institutions of higher education to disclose to a parent or legal guardian information regarding a student’s violation of any law or institutional rule or policy governing the use or possession of alcohol or a controlled substance if the student is under 21 and the institution determines that the student has committed a disciplinary violation with respect to the use or possession.       Since 1998 Congress has enacted two additional exceptions to the statutory prior consent rule:      1)     The 2000 Campus Sex Crimes Prevention Act added a new subsection (b)(7) to the statute to ensure that an educational institution may disclose information concerning registered sex offenders provided to it under State sex offender registration and community notification programs.   2)     The USA Patriot Act of 2001 added a new subsection (j) that allows the U.S Attorney General to apply for an ex parte court order requiring an educational agency or institution and prosecutions of specified crimes or acts of terrorism (domestic or international). The Attorney General must certify that there are specific facts giving reason to believe that the records are likely to contain the required information. requests.request_text: Pursuant to the California Public Records Act, Government Code § 7920.000 et seq., I request electronic copies of the records described below concerning contracts, purchase orders, and other procurement agreements of City and County of San Francisco with a total authorized, cumulative, not-to-exceed, or potential value exceeding $10,000.   Time Period: January 1, 2022 through the date of the agency's response.   For purposes of this request, "Agency" means City and County of San Francisco.   For purposes of this request, "contract" should be interpreted to include contracts, agreements, professional or consulting services agreements, purchase orders, master agreements, public works contracts, software/SaaS agreements, equipment agreements, service agreements, amendments, extensions, renewals, change orders, task orders, cooperative procurements, and piggyback procurements.   This request includes agreements:   originally valued above $10,000;  whose cumulative value exceeded $10,000 through amendments, change orders, renewals, extensions, purchase orders, or other modifications; or  whose maximum authorized or reasonably ascertainable potential value exceeds $10,000.   1. Agencywide Contract Register / Procurement Data   Please provide any existing contract register, procurement database export, ERP report, purchasing report, accounts-payable/procurement report, or other existing record sufficient to identify responsive contracts.   To the extent maintained, please provide the following fields:   Contract, agreement, or purchase order number  Solicitation number  Vendor/contractor name  Department, division, office, or agency unit  Description or scope  Contract type  Original contract amount  Current or cumulative authorized amount  Amount paid to date  Contract execution date  Effective/start date  Expiration/end date  Amendment/change-order amounts  Procurement method  Funding source, where maintained  Governing-body agenda/item number, where applicable  Contract status   Please provide structured data in its existing native electronic format, such as Excel, CSV, or comparable machine-readable format, rather than converting it to PDF where reasonably available.   I am requesting existing records or data exports and am not asking the Agency to create a new record if one does not already exist.   2. Executed Contracts and Amendments   For each responsive contract, please provide:   The executed contract, agreement, purchase order, or other award document;  All amendments, modifications, extensions, renewals, task orders, and change orders;  Exhibits, schedules, or statements of work establishing scope and compensation; and  Records sufficient to show the total amount actually paid under the contract.   3. Solicitation and Competitive Procurement Records   For contracts resulting from a competitive procurement, please provide:   Request for Proposal, Request for Bid, Request for Qualifications, Request for Quotation, Invitation for Bid, or other solicitation;  Amendments and addenda to the solicitation;  Records identifying vendors that submitted bids, proposals, quotations, or responses;  Submitted bids or proposals;  Bid tabulations or price comparisons;  Evaluation and selection criteria;  Evaluator scoring sheets or consolidated scoring records;  Evaluation committee recommendations;  Award recommendation or notice of intent to award; and  Records concerning any formal bid or procurement protest and its disposition.   I am seeking records documenting the procurement, evaluation, selection, and award process rather than general correspondence unrelated to the award.   4. Noncompetitive, Sole-Source, Emergency, and Cooperative Procurements   For responsive contracts that were not awarded through an open competitive process, please provide records sufficient to identify the basis for the procurement method, including, as applicable:   Sole-source or single-source justification;  Competition waiver or exemption;  Emergency procurement justification;  Findings, determinations, or approvals authorizing a noncompetitive procurement;  Cooperative purchasing, piggyback, or governmental-contract authority relied upon;  The originating solicitation and contract relied upon for a cooperative or piggyback procurement, where maintained;  Written price-reasonableness determinations;  Vendor-selection justifications; and  Any other procurement exception or waiver documentation.   5. Retroactive Contracts, Ratifications, and After-the-Fact Approvals   Please provide records identifying any responsive contract, amendment, extension, renewal, purchase order, change order, or other agreement during the requested period that:   Was executed or approved after its stated effective date;  Was executed or approved after the contractor began providing goods or services;  Was submitted to the Agency's governing body or another approving authority for retroactive approval;  Ratified or memorialized services, purchases, commitments, or obligations that had already occurred;  Was described as retroactive, a ratification, confirming purchase order, after-the-fact approval, or unauthorized commitment; or  Otherwise required subsequent approval because goods or services were ordered or performed before the required contractual or procurement authorization was completed.   For each such transaction, please provide the agreement or amendment and any staff report, agenda report, memorandum, justification, approval form, procurement record, or other document explaining the circumstances and basis for the retroactive or after-the-fact approval.   6. Contract Award and Approval Records   For each responsive contract, please provide any readily identifiable:   Governing-body staff report, agenda report, or agenda item;  Award recommendation;  Approval memorandum;  Delegated-authority approval;  Procurement approval or exception form;  Fiscal or budget approval associated with the award; and  Records identifying the official, employee, governing body, or other authority that approved the award.   For purposes of this section, "governing body" includes the Agency's applicable governing authority, such as a City Council, Board of Supervisors, board of directors, commission, or other approving body.   7. Vendor Performance and Contract Compliance   To the extent maintained in the contract, procurement, or vendor file, please provide:   Vendor or contractor performance evaluations;  Corrective-action notices;  Cure notices;  Notices of deficiency or nonperformance;  Default notices;  Suspension or debarment records associated with the contract;  Termination notices; and  Records documenting liquidated damages, credits, refunds, repayment demands, withheld payments, or other financial remedies associated with contractor performance.   8. Procurement Value Changes   For responsive contracts, please provide existing records sufficient to identify changes between the original award value and the current or final authorized value, including amendments, renewals, extensions, task orders, purchase orders, and change orders that increased the Agency's financial commitment.   This includes contracts whose original value was below $10,000 but whose cumulative authorized value subsequently exceeded $10,000.   Production Format and Scope   Please provide responsive records electronically and in their native electronic format where reasonably available.   For spreadsheets, databases, contract registers, ERP exports, or similar structured records, please provide Excel, CSV, or another comparable machine-readable format rather than converting structured data into PDF.   If responsive records are maintained by multiple departments, offices, divisions, procurement units, or other components of the Agency, please coordinate the request with the appropriate custodians so that the response is not limited solely to records maintained by the office initially receiving this request.   Given the potential volume of responsive materials, I welcome rolling production, with priority given to:   The Agencywide contract/procurement data requested in Section 1;  Noncompetitive, sole-source, emergency, cooperative, and retroactive procurement records requested in Sections 4 and 5;  Records showing contract value increases requested in Section 8; and  The remaining contract, solicitation, award, and performance records.   If producing all underlying contract files simultaneously would cause substantial delay, please produce the structured contract register or procurement data first while the remaining records are being gathered.   If the Agency believes any portion of this request is unclear or would benefit from reasonable refinement, please contact me so that the scope may be clarified without unnecessarily delaying production.   If any responsive record or portion of a record is withheld, please identify the specific statutory basis for withholding and produce all reasonably segregable nonexempt portions.   Please confirm receipt of this request and provide the Agency's determination regarding responsive and disclosable records pursuant to the California Public Records Act.   Thank you.

Dear Controller’s Office:   We are writing to request records pursuant to the California Public Records Act (“CPRA”),[1] the San Francisco Sunshine Ordinance[2], and the California Constitution.[3] We seek disclosure of records related to the review of the Initiative Ordinance – Illegal Substance Dependence Screening and Treatment for Recipients of City Public Assistance (“Measure F”) by the San Francisco Controller’s Office (“Controller”). [4] We also seek documents related to the Controller’s reviews of the San Francisco Humans Services Agency’s administration of the County Adult Assistance Program (“CAAP”).   We hereby request the following records in the possession of the Controller:  (1) d For the period January 1, 2021 to present, all evaluations by the Controller of the San Francisco Human Service Agency’s provision of in-kind aid, as required by SFMC Sec. 20.7-56.  (2) All documents used by the Controller’s Office in preparation of the December 11, 2023 Controller’s letter regarding Measure F.  (3) For the period January 1, 2021 to present, All evaluations of the San Francisco Human Service Agency’s implementation of CAAP.   In responding to this Request, please note that the CPRA broadly defines the term “record.” Specifically, the term includes “any writing containing information relating to the conduct of the people’s business prepared, owned, used, or retained by any state or local agency regardless of physical form or characteristics.”[5] The CPRA defines, in turn, a “writing” as any “means of recording upon any tangible thing any form of communication or representation.”[6] This Request therefore applies to all paper documents, as well as to all emails, videos, audio recordings, text messages, or other electronic records within the Controller’s possession or control. Even if a record was created by a member of another government agency or a member of the public, it still must be produced so long as it is (or was) “used” or “retained” by the Controller.[7]   As permitted by the CPRA, this Request sets forth the specific categories of information that we are seeking, rather than asks for documents by name.[8] It is your obligation to conduct record searches based on the criteria identified herein.[9] But should you come to believe that the present Request is overly broad, you are required to (1) offer assistance in identifying responsive records and information; (2) describe “the information technology and physical location in which the records exist;” and (3) provide “suggestions for overcoming any practical basis” that you assert as a reason to delay or deny access to the records or information sought.[10]   The CPRA requires that you respond to this Request in ten days.[11] If you contend that an express provision of law exempts a responsive record from disclosure, either in whole or in part, you must make that determination in writing. Such a determination must specify the legal authority on which you rely and must identify both the name and title of the person(s) responsible for the determination not to disclose.[12] Additionally, even if you contend that a portion of a record requested is exempt from disclosure, you still must release the non-exempt portion of that record.[13] Please note that the CPRA “endows” the Controller with “discretionary authority to override” any of the Act’s statutory exemptions “when a dominating public interest favors disclosure.”[14] Lastly, please provide complete documents, even if only a portion of a document is responsive to this request; for example, provide all attachments to memoranda.   Because the ACLU is a non-profit organization and because this Request pertains to a matter of public concern, we request a fee waiver. None of the information obtained will be sold or distributed for profit. We also request that, to the extent possible, documents be provided in electronic format; the CPRA requires documents to be produced in electronic format wherever possible.[15] Doing so will eliminate the need to copy the materials and provides another basis for the requested fee-waiver. If, however, you are unwilling to waive costs and anticipate that costs will exceed $50, or that the time needed to copy the records will delay their release, please contact us so that we can arrange to inspect the documents or decide which documents we wish to have copied and produced. Otherwise, please copy and send all responsive records as soon as possible, and—if necessary—on a rolling basis, to dvernercrist@aclunc.org or 39 Drumm Street, San Francisco, CA 94111.   Thank you in advance for your assistance with this Request. We look forward to receiving your response within ten days. And once again, if you require any clarification of this Request, please let us know.   Best,   Dylan Verner-Crist  Investigator (Lead)  ACLU Foundation of Northern California  dvernercrist@aclunc.org  916-252-7930     [1] Gov’t Code §§ 7920 et seq.  [2] S.F. Admin. Code § 67.1 et seq.  [3] Cal. Const., art. I, § 3(b)(2).  [4] See the City and County of San Francisco’s page on Measure F, available at https://voterguide.sfelections.org/local-ballot-measures/measure-f.  [5] Gov’t Code § 7920.530(a).  [6] Id. § 7920.545.   [7] Id. § 7920.530(a); see California State Univ. v. Superior Ct., 90 Cal. App. 4th 810, 824–25 (2001) (concluding that documents which were “unquestionably ‘used’ and/or ‘retained’ by [an agency]” were public records); see also Cty. of Santa Clara v. Superior Ct., 170 Cal. App. 4th 1301, 1334 (2009) (“[W]hile section 6254.9 recognizes the availability of copyright protection for software in a proper case, it provides no statutory authority for asserting any other copyright interest.”).  [8] Gov’t Code § 7922.530(a).  [9] See id. § 7922.535; see also Cty. of San Jose v. Superior Ct., 2 Cal. 5th 608, 627 (2017).  [10] Gov’t Code § 7922.600(a).  [11] Id. § 7922.535(a).  [12] Id. § 7922; see also id. § 7922.540.  [13] Id. § 7922.525(b); id. § 7922.535(a).  [14] CBS, Inc. v. Block, 42 Cal. 3d 646, 652 (1986); see also Nat’l Conf. of Black Mayors v. Chico Cmty. Publ’g, Inc., 25 Cal. App. 5th 570, 579 (2018) (construing the CPRA’s exemptions as “permissive, not mandatory—they allow nondisclosure but do not prohibit disclosure”).  [15] Gov’t Code § 7922.570.

IMMEDIATE DISCLOSURE REQUEST   San Francisco Administrative Code section 67.25(a)      Real Estate AI Studio   4539 N 22nd St Ste N   Phoenix, AZ 85016   kevin@realestateaistudio.com      26 August 2026      City and County of San Francisco   Department of Building Inspection, Housing Inspection Services Division   49 South Van Ness Avenue, 4th Floor      Submitted via: NextRequest portal at sanfrancisco.nextrequest.com,   department: Building Inspection   (program contact: dbi.hissection604@sfgov.org)      Re: California Public Records Act request. Exterior elevated element (balcony)      inspection records, Health and Safety Code section 17973 and Civil Code      section 5551.      To the custodian of records,      Health and Safety Code section 17973(d)(1) requires an inspector who   finds that an   exterior elevated element poses an immediate threat, or that immediate repairs,   shoring or prevention of occupant access are necessary, to provide a   copy of that   report to the local enforcement agency within 15 days. Civil Code   section 5551(g)(1)   imposes a parallel duty for common interest developments. Section   17973(d)(1) further   provides that a local enforcement agency may require a copy of the   initial or final   report to be submitted to the local jurisdiction.      This request seeks the records the Housing Inspection Services   Division therefore   holds, and in particular any log or index by which it tracks them.      RECORDS SOUGHT      This is a request under the California Public Records Act, Government   Code section   7920.000 et seq. Please treat each numbered item as severable. That one item may   require more time does not justify withholding another (Gov. Code sec.   7922.535(a)).      Item 1. Tracking log or database of covered buildings. PRIORITY ITEM.      Any log, register, roster, index, tracking spreadsheet, case   management extract or   database table by which the Department tracks buildings subject to   Health and Safety   Code section 17973 and/or Civil Code section 5551 and San Francisco Housing Code   section 604, and their compliance status.      Please produce this record as it is currently maintained, in the   electronic format in   which the agency holds it (Gov. Code sec. 7922.570(b)(1)), or in any   export format the   agency already uses for its own purposes or for provision to other   agencies, such as a   standard CSV or XLSX report from the Department's permit and case   management system   (Gov. Code sec. 7922.570(b)(2)).      I do not request that the agency construct a new record, write a new   query, or perform   any programming. I request a copy of an existing record, or an existing standard   export of one. Accordingly the cost limitations of Gov. Code sections   7922.530(a) and   7922.575(a) apply, and section 7922.575(b)(2) does not.      To the extent the record contains them, I seek these fields: property address;   assessor parcel number; case, permit or record number; date the report   or affidavit   was received; name and license number of the inspecting professional; whether an   immediate threat or emergency condition was reported; the number and   type of exterior   elevated elements inspected and found deficient; compliance status;   the date of any   notice, order to comply or re-inspection; and the date of any   abatement or clearance.      If any single field is deemed exempt, please redact that field and produce the   remaining columns (Gov. Code sec. 7922.525(b)).      Item 2. Index of filings received, and of properties that have not filed.      A list or export identifying every Compliance Affidavit filed under   San Francisco   Housing Code section 604 received by the Department from 1 January 2019 to the   present, showing property address, date received and filing status.      Separately, any list of properties identified as delinquent,   non-compliant or non-   filing, and any notice of violation, order to comply or referral   issued for failure to   file.      Item 3. Governing internal guidance.      Any final policy, procedure, standard operating procedure, intake   instruction, staff   bulletin, form or written guidance governing how the Department   receives, logs, routes   and acts on reports made under Health and Safety Code section   17973(d)(1) or Civil   Code section 5551(g)(1). This item seeks final operative guidance only, not   predecisional drafts.      SCOPE I AM NOT ASKING FOR      To narrow the review burden and remove any privacy question at the   outset, I am not   requesting individual unit numbers, occupant names, occupant contact details, or   occupant complaint narratives. Please redact those wherever they   appear rather than   withholding a record on their account.      FORMAT AND FEES      Please produce all records electronically, by email or portal   download, pursuant to   Gov. Code section 7922.570. Public records do not lose their status   because they are   stored in a computer (Gov. Code sec. 7922.585(d)).      I am not requesting paper copies, and I do not authorise any cost.   Please treat this   as a request for electronic delivery at no charge.      Where a record is produced electronically from an existing file, the   direct cost of   duplication under Gov. Code section 7922.530(a) is nil, and the cost   of producing an   electronic copy under section 7922.575(a) is limited to the direct   cost of producing   that copy, which for an emailed file is likewise nil. I am not asking   the Department   to compile, extract or program anything, so section 7922.575(b)(2)   does not apply.      If the Department believes any charge would nonetheless attach to any   item, please do   not incur it. Tell me what the charge would be and for which item, and   I will either   narrow that item or withdraw it. Please continue to process the   remaining items in the   meantime, which sections 7922.535(a) and 7922.525(b) require in any event.      ASSISTANCE      If any item is unclear, or if the Department contends an item does not   reasonably   describe an identifiable record, Gov. Code section 7922.600(a)   requires the Department   to assist me in identifying responsive records, to describe the   information technology   and physical location in which the records exist, and to suggest means   of overcoming   any practical basis for denial. Please do that rather than denying the item. In   particular, please identify the system of record in which exterior   elevated element   reports and compliance status are maintained.      WITHHOLDING      Any denial must be in writing and must set forth the names and titles   or positions of   each person responsible for it (Gov. Code sec. 7922.540). Any   withholding must be   justified under Gov. Code section 7922.000, and any reasonably   segregable portion must   be released (Gov. Code sec. 7922.525(b)). Under Gov. Code section 7921.005 the   Department may not permit a building owner, association or inspector   to control the   disclosure of otherwise disclosable records.      I look forward to your determination within 10 days (Gov. Code sec.   7922.535(a)). Any   extension must comply with section 7922.535(b) and (c) and may not   exceed 14 days.      IMMEDIATE DISCLOSURE REQUEST, specific to San Francisco.      Item 1 and Item 2 of this request are submitted as an IMMEDIATE   DISCLOSURE REQUEST   under San Francisco Administrative Code section 67.25(a). Both seek an   existing log or   index rather than a document review, and are therefore simple, routine   and readily   answerable within the meaning of that section. A response is due no   later than the   close of business on the day following the day of this request.      Item 2B. Delinquency records, specific to San Francisco.      The Department's own notice regarding Housing Code section 604 states that code   enforcement will be initiated against property owners who do not file   a compliance   affidavit. That presupposes a list of who has not filed.      I request any list of properties for which section 604 code   enforcement proceedings   have been initiated for failure to file, and any list of properties   identified as   delinquent in filing.      Thank you for your assistance. I am happy to narrow or clarify any   item, and would   rather have a conversation about scope than receive a denial.

Public Record Request   This is a follow up to the SOTF Complaint Committee hearing on 12/21/2021. The first 4 items are rewrites and expanded of issues in my SOTF complaint File #21144 but in public record request form. This being written with SOTF in mind.   I concede that the two of you are probably better at search than I am, but I do not think I am as neophyte as Ms. Gerull seemed to insinuate at the hearing. I do appreciate the offer of a NextRequest search tutorial that was made at the hearing, but let's see how well you and NextRequest do.   Since the Department of Technology is the controlling/contracted department of the City and County of San Francisco with NextRequest, all records that are put on the San Francisco NextRequest portal are the responsibility and should be accessible by the Department of Technology. The Department of Technology is responsible for public record searches returning all records that meet the criteria of a search or the Department of Technology violates Sec 67.21 (a), CPRA 6253 (b), CPRA 6253.3 and CPRA 6253.10 (a). Neither the Sunshine Ordinance or the CPRA requires the use of "Public Record Request" words to inspect public records and public information. A search of the San Francisco NextRequest portal is a request for the inspect public records and public information  Sec 67.21 (a)  Every person having custody of any public record or public information, as defined herein, (hereinafter referred to as a custodian of a public record) shall, at normal times and during normal and reasonable hours of operation, without unreasonable delay, and without requiring an appointment, permit the public record, or any segregable portion of a record, to be inspected and examined by any person.
